project.title: RateGuard: Distributed Rate Limiter with Redis, Lua and an AI Policy Advisor
project.tagline: Build a multi-tenant rate-limiting service whose limits hold across every instance, survive a Redis outage and never over-admit, with AI as your pair programmer
project.description: Over nine phases you build RateGuard like a professional team: requirements and threats, design with ADRs, a test-first implementation of a token bucket and a sliding window counter as pure functions and as atomic Redis Lua scripts that use one clock, a Redis Cluster-ready key layout with hash tags, tenants with SHA-256 hashed API keys and a constant-time admin token, the standard rate-limit headers and Retry-After, per-minute usage statistics and an AI policy advisor with an offline fallback, integration tests that race parallel requests for the last token, CI/CD with GitHub Actions, Docker, optional free-tier deployment, a game day that freezes Redis, a circuit breaker with per-tenant fail modes, observability and a retrospective. Pick Java, Python or TypeScript; the spec, the Lua scripts and the tests are shared. Everything runs on your laptop, and the AI feature works offline.

outcomes: Turn a multi-tenant API brief into testable requirements, user stories and a threat list (stolen keys, over-admission across instances, key-pattern injection, retry storms)
Compare rate-limiting algorithms and implement a token bucket and a sliding window counter as pure, exhaustively tested functions
Make limiter decisions atomic across instances with Redis Lua scripts, one clock (Redis TIME) and parity tests against the pure functions
Design a Redis key layout that is Redis Cluster ready (hash tags), expires idle state and never uses KEYS
Secure a service with hashed, rotatable API keys and a constant-time admin token, and prove every refusal with tests
Add an AI policy advisor whose output is validated, never auto-applied and falls back to deterministic rules offline
Build CI/CD with GitHub Actions: matrix, caching, reusable workflows, Redis service containers, GHCR
Run a game day that freezes Redis, write a blameless post-mortem and add a circuit breaker with per-tenant fail modes
Add request IDs, JSON logs and metrics, and keep v1.0 and v1.1 data compatible both ways
Use AI assistants deliberately and verify every output
project.ai_feature: AI policy advisor: reads a tenant's per-minute usage statistics and suggests KEEP, RAISE_LIMIT, LOWER_LIMIT or INVESTIGATE with a plain-language summary. Offline deterministic rules by default, optional Ollama or a free Gemini/Groq key; the output is validated, never applied automatically, and no rate-limit decision depends on the AI
project.portfolio_blurb: Built RateGuard, a multi-tenant distributed rate limiter: token bucket and sliding window counter as pure functions and as atomic Redis Lua scripts (parity-tested, Redis TIME as the only clock), proven by parallel requests across instances to never over-admit; a Redis Cluster-ready key layout with hash tags; SHA-256 hashed, rotatable API keys; standard rate-limit headers; an AI policy advisor with validated output and offline fallback; >=85 % test coverage; GitHub Actions CI/CD to GHCR; Docker; and, after a game day that froze Redis, a circuit breaker with per-tenant fail modes (closed, open, local), request IDs, JSON logs and metrics.

phases.title: Setup and orientation
phases.heading: Phase 0 · Setup and orientation
phases.why_md:
Every professional project starts with a working local environment and a clean Git workflow. Teams
lose days to "works on my machine". In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, start
Redis, run the starter, meet the test suite that will guide you, open your first pull request and
start your `AI_LOG.md`. That is the evidence a reviewer looks for first: a repo that builds from a
clean checkout with one command.
objectives: Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
Pick a track (Java, Python or TypeScript) and install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux.
Start Redis with Docker Compose, talk to it with `redis-cli` and run the starter so `GET /health` returns `UP`.
Run lint and tests locally and see which tests are *pending* and why.
Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

steps.title: Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
steps.content_md:
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/distributed-rate-limiter` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**.
   The `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/distributed-rate-limiter.git
   cd distributed-rate-limiter
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/distributed-rate-limiter.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # you should see phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/distributed-rate-limiter`), not under `/mnt/c`. File watching and Docker volumes are 5–10× faster there.

steps.title: Start Redis and say hello to it
steps.content_md:
```bash
docker compose up -d redis
docker compose ps                         # redis should be "healthy"
docker compose exec redis redis-cli ping  # PONG
docker compose exec redis redis-cli INCR hello   # (integer) 1 - run it again: 2
docker compose exec redis redis-cli DEL hello
```
`INCR` is atomic: a hundred clients incrementing the same key at once get a hundred different
numbers. Keep that in mind; the whole project is about making *more complex* decisions just as
atomic. Redis keeps 16 numbered databases: your app uses database `0`, the integration tests use
database `15` and **empty it before each test**, so tests never touch your dev data. Port 6379
already taken (another Redis)? Set `REDIS_PORT=56379` in `.env` and use that port in `REDIS_URL`
(and `TEST_REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:56379/15` for the tests).

steps.content_md:
```bash
make lint test
```
You will see **a few passing tests** (`/health`) and well over a hundred **skipped** ones. They are
*pending*: the complete test suite for RateGuard is already written and switched off in one file per track:

| Track | Pending list |
|---|---|
| Java | `tracks/java/src/test/java/org/aicancode/rateguard/support/Pending.java` |
| Python | `tracks/python/tests/conftest.py` (`PENDING`) |
| TypeScript | `tracks/typescript/test/pending.ts` (`PENDING`) |

Open the list now. Each entry names a milestone ("Phase 3 M2 - token bucket"). In Phase 3 you delete
one entry at a time, watch the tests go red, and make them green.

steps.title: Your first pull request
steps.content_md:
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant helped you install the toolchain and
   how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab. Forks have Actions switched off until you click **"I understand my
   workflows, go ahead and enable them"**. The CI workflow runs lint + unit tests for all three tracks.
   Wait for green, fill in the PR template and merge.

quiz.q: Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
options: Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
Otherwise the `solution` branch and phase tags are missing from your fork
Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
Otherwise Docker Compose cannot find Redis
quiz.explanation: Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

quiz.q: On Windows, where should the repository live?
options: `C:\Users\you\distributed-rate-limiter`, opened from WSL as `/mnt/c/Users/you/distributed-rate-limiter`
Inside the WSL2 Linux file system, e.g. `~/code/distributed-rate-limiter`
On a network drive so Docker can share it
It does not matter
quiz.explanation: Cross-file-system access from WSL to `/mnt/c` is slow and breaks file watching. Keep code in the Linux file system and open it with VS Code's WSL extension.

quiz.q: Why do the integration tests use Redis database 15 instead of database 0?
options: Redis allows only one client per database
The tests empty their database (`FLUSHDB`) before each test, which must never touch your dev data
Database 15 is faster
CI cannot reach database 0
quiz.explanation: Integration tests start from a known, empty state. A separate numbered database makes that safe on your laptop. Point `TEST_REDIS_URL` only at a Redis you own: `FLUSHDB` on someone else's database is a real incident.

quiz.q: Why are most tests skipped in the starter?
options: They are flaky
CI is too slow to run them
They describe behaviour you will implement in Phases 3–4 and are switched on one milestone at a time
They only run on the solution branch
quiz.explanation: The full suite is written up-front (a test-first workflow). Deleting a line from the pending list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

quiz.q: Which of these should never go into an AI prompt?
options: The output of `scripts/doctor.sh`
A stack trace from your own code
Your `.env` file with the admin token and an LLM API key
The OpenAPI spec
quiz.explanation: Secrets never go into prompts. Anyone with the admin token can create tenants, read their usage and reset their limits. Redact before you paste.

quiz.q: `INCR hello` run by 100 clients at the same moment ends at exactly 100. Why?
options: Redis queues clients by IP address
Redis executes commands one at a time, so each `INCR` is an atomic read-modify-write
Docker serialises network traffic
The value is only approximate; it could end lower
quiz.explanation: Redis runs commands (and, as you will see in Phase 2, whole Lua scripts) one after another on a single thread. A read in the app followed by a write from the app is *not* atomic: another client can run in between.

phases.title: Requirements, threats and user stories
phases.heading: Phase 1 · Requirements, threats and user stories
phases.why_md:
Most failed projects fail before the first line of code: nobody wrote down what "done" means. A
rate limiter adds two questions that are easy to skip and expensive to get wrong: **what exactly is
"100 per minute"** (a fixed minute? any 60 seconds? may a client burst?) and **what happens when
the limiter itself is in trouble**? A short, testable requirements document with an explicit threat
list gives every test a reason to exist, lets you say *no* to scope creep, and is the first thing an
interviewer asks about ("design a rate limiter" is one of the most common system-design questions).
AI assistants are great at drafting requirements, and just as good at inventing requirements nobody
asked for. Your job is to keep the ones you can test.
objectives: Turn a one-paragraph brief into numbered **functional** (FR) and **measurable non-functional** (NFR) requirements.
Map personas (and one system: the tenant's backend instances) to **credentials** and write down who may do what.
List at least six **threats** (abuse cases and failure cases) and the requirement that answers each.
Write 8–10 **user stories** with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and create them as GitHub Issues.
Write an explicit **out-of-scope** list and a **back-of-the-envelope estimate** of checks per second and Redis load.

steps.title: Read the brief and the contract
steps.content_md:
> *Build RateGuard: a rate-limiting service for a small API company whose customers ("tenants") share
> one backend. The operator creates tenants, gives each an API key and a policy ("100 requests per
> minute"), can change policies and replace leaked keys at any time, and wants to see who uses how
> much. The company's backend runs on several instances, in more than one language, and asks
> RateGuard before doing work; the limit must hold for the tenant as a whole. Clients must be told
> exactly when to retry. Some operations cost more than others. AI may suggest better policies from
> the usage numbers, but must never change anything by itself, and the limiter must work without it.
> It must run on a laptop for free.*

Open `spec/openapi.yaml`. The HTTP contract is **given** so the three tracks stay compatible; your
requirements must be consistent with it (status codes, limits, the `problem+json` error format, the
two `securitySchemes`, the `X-RateLimit-*` and `Retry-After` headers).

steps.title: Personas and the permission matrix
steps.content_md:
Write at least three personas, e.g. *Meera, the operator*; *Ravi, a developer at a tenant*; and **the
API company's backend instances**: not people, but the callers of `/limits/check` on every request.
Then fill a matrix: rows = actions (health, create/read/delete tenants, change a policy, rotate a key,
reset, usage, advice, check, demo), columns = anonymous, tenant key, admin token. Every "no" in this
table becomes a test in Phase 3. Notice that the check request contains **no tenant id**: the key
decides which tenant you are. Ask yourself why that removes a whole class of bugs.

steps.title: Functional requirements
steps.content_md:
In `spec/requirements.md` write FR-1 … FR-n as "The system shall …" statements. Each needs a number
or a status code, so a test can check it. Bad: *"Limits are enforced fairly."* Good: *"With a token
bucket of 5 per 60 s, the 6th check within the same second is denied with `retryAfterMs` = 12 000."*
Cover admin authentication, tenants and policies, API keys (issue once, hash, rotate), the two
algorithms, the check and demo endpoints, the headers, reset, usage, the advisor, errors and health.

The algorithms deserve their own requirements. Write down **what state each keeps** and **the exact
decision rule**: a token bucket refills `limit` tokens per window continuously and starts full; a
sliding window counter weights the previous fixed window by how much of it is still inside the
sliding window. If you leave this open, three tracks will disagree by one request at a window edge
and every test that counts "allowed" becomes flaky.

steps.title: Non-functional requirements and threats
steps.content_md:
Cover correctness across instances, clocks, latency, behaviour when Redis is slow or down, security,
memory, AI independence, cost and portability. Make each one measurable: *"with 3 instances and 50
parallel checks against a limit of 10, exactly 10 are allowed"*, *"a check adds < 5 ms p95"*, *"a
Redis command slower than 1 000 ms is a failure, and a failure is never an 'allowed'"*.

Then the threat list. For each abuse or failure case, name the requirement that stops it:

| Threat | Answer |
|---|---|
| A Redis backup leaks every tenant's API key | store only a SHA-256 hash of each key (FR-5) |
| Two instances both admit the "last" request | one atomic decision in Redis per check (NFR-1) |
| `{"cost": -5}` refills the bucket | cost validated 1–1 000, cost > limit is `422` (FR-9) |
| A tenant id like `acme*` or `a}{b` reaches other tenants' keys | strict id and resource character sets (FR-2, FR-9) |
| A leaked key keeps working | rotation refuses the old key immediately (FR-5) |
| Redis hangs and every request waits forever | timeout + fail closed with `503` and `Retry-After` (NFR-3, NFR-4) |

steps.title: User stories → GitHub Issues
steps.content_md:
For each story use the **User story** issue template (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user_story.yml`). It asks
for the story, the acceptance criteria and the Phase 3 milestone. Label them `user-story`. With the
GitHub CLI:
```bash

quiz.q: Which requirement is testable?
options: "The limiter should be fast."
"Limits must be fair to all tenants."
"With a token bucket of 5 per 60 s, a 6th check in the same second is denied with retryAfterMs = 12000."
"The service should handle bursts."
quiz.explanation: It has an exact rule a unit test can check with numbers: one token refills every 60 000 / 5 = 12 000 ms. The others need a measurable threshold first.

quiz.q: Why does `POST /limits/check` contain no tenant id?
options: To keep the request small
The API key identifies the tenant, so a caller can never check (or spend) another tenant's limit by changing an id
Tenant ids are secret
Redis cannot look up ids
quiz.explanation: If the id were in the body, every handler would need to check "does this key belong to this id?", and the one that forgets is a broken-object-level-authorisation bug (OWASP API1). Without an id there is nothing to forget.

quiz.q: Three app instances each keep a limit of 100 per minute in their own memory. What does a tenant really get?
options: 100 per minute
33 per minute per instance
Up to 300 per minute, depending on how the load balancer spreads the requests
It depends on the algorithm only
quiz.explanation: Each instance counts only what it sees. That is why the state must live in one shared place (Redis) and the decision must be atomic there (NFR-1).

quiz.q: Why is a denied `/limits/check` a `200` with `allowed: false`, while the demo endpoint answers `429`?
options: It is a mistake in the contract
The check endpoint answers a question ("may I?") successfully either way; the demo endpoint is the protected resource itself, so it refuses the request
`429` is not allowed for POST requests
Clients cannot read `429` bodies
quiz.explanation: The caller of `/limits/check` is a backend that wants the full decision (remaining, retry time) and decides itself; an end client of a protected endpoint needs the standard `429` + `Retry-After`.

quiz.q: Your estimate says ~6 000 Redis commands per second at peak. What does that mean for the design?
options: You need Redis Cluster from day one
One Redis instance is plenty; spend the effort on atomicity and on behaviour when Redis is unavailable
You must cache decisions in the app
You need a message queue in front of Redis
quiz.explanation: A single Redis handles roughly 100 000 simple commands per second. What breaks limiters is concurrency between instances and a slow or missing Redis, not volume. The key layout can still be made cluster-ready cheaply (Phase 2).

quiz.q: An AI draft adds "FR-17: the advisor applies its suggested limit automatically every night". What do you do?
options: Keep it, automation is good
Remove it: the brief says AI must never change anything by itself, and an attacker who controls usage patterns could steer an automatic change
Keep it, but only for RAISE_LIMIT
Ask the AI if it is safe
quiz.explanation: Requirements come from the brief, not from the assistant's idea of a smart product. A human applies advice with `PUT /policy`; log the rejection in `AI_LOG.md`.

Defining algorithms precisely enough that three implementations agree to the request.
Threat modelling that includes failure cases: races between instances, clock drift, a slow Redis.
User stories with refusal criteria, tracked as GitHub Issues, and estimates that keep the design simple.

phases.title: Design (algorithms, Lua scripts, key layout, failure policy, API contract)
phases.heading: Phase 2 · Design: algorithms, Lua scripts, key layout, failure policy, API contract
phases.why_md:
Design is where you make the expensive decisions on purpose: which algorithm defines "100 per
minute", where the decision is made so that three instances cannot over-admit, whose clock counts,
how keys are laid out so the data can move to a cluster later, how credentials are stored, and what
the service does when Redis is not there. Writing them down as diagrams and **Architecture Decision
Records (ADRs)** lets a reviewer follow your reasoning in minutes. The two **Lua scripts** are the one
artefact shared by all three tracks, so a mistake here costs three times, and a read-then-write
outside a script is an over-admission bug waiting for a traffic spike.
objectives: Draw context, container and check-sequence diagrams and a Redis key table in Mermaid / Markdown.
Compare token bucket, sliding window log, sliding window counter and fixed window, and pick two.
Write five ADRs: atomic Lua scripts with pure-function twins, Redis `TIME` as the clock, hash tags in keys, fail closed, hashed API keys + constant-time admin token.
Write `spec/lua/token_bucket.lua` and `spec/lua/sliding_window.lua` and run them by hand with `redis-cli`.
Read the given OpenAPI contract and map each endpoint to a requirement.

steps.title: Diagrams in `spec/architecture.md`
steps.content_md:
Mermaid is text, so it diffs and reviews like code. Start with a container diagram:
```text
flowchart TB
    lb["Load balancer"] --> a1["RateGuard (Java)"] & a2["RateGuard (Python)"] & a3["RateGuard (TS)"]
    a1 & a2 & a3 -- "EVALSHA (atomic)" --> redis[("Redis 7")]
    a1 & a2 & a3 -. "advice only, timeout + fallback" .-> llm[("LLM endpoint")]
```
Wrap it in a code fence with the language `mermaid` and preview it on GitHub or in VS Code (extension
"Markdown Preview Mermaid Support"). Then draw:
1. **The check sequence**: key lookup, tenant lookup, one script call, the headers; then two instances
   racing for the last token. Where exactly is the race decided?
2. **A key table**: every Redis key, its type, its TTL and who writes it.
3. **Failure modes**: Redis refused, Redis frozen, Redis restarted, scripts flushed, the LLM down.
   For each, what does the client see?

steps.title: Choose the algorithms
steps.content_md:
Work these four by hand for a limit of 3 per 60 s and requests at 0:59, 0:59, 0:59, 1:01:

| Algorithm | State | 4th request at 1:01? | Memory |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed window (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`) | one counter per window | allowed: a new window started (6 in 2 s!) | tiny |
| Sliding window log | a sorted set of every timestamp | denied | one entry per request |
| Sliding window counter | `cur`, `prev`, window index | denied, retry in 19 s | 3 numbers |
| Token bucket | `tokens`, `ts` | allowed only if a token refilled | 2 numbers |

RateGuard offers the **token bucket** (allows bursts after idle time, the most common API policy) and
the **sliding window counter** (smooth, never more than the limit in a window, constant memory), per
tenant. Write the exact maths into `architecture.md`. Two details decide whether three languages
agree: the sliding window keeps its maths in **integers** by multiplying everything by `window_ms`,
and both algorithms must say what happens when the clock goes **backwards**.

steps.title: ADRs
steps.content_md:
Copy `spec/adr/0000-template.md` five times:
1. `0001-atomic-lua-scripts-with-pure-function-twins.md`: read-decide-write from the app vs
   `WATCH`/`MULTI` vs `INCR` vs a Lua script. Why also keep the same maths as pure functions?
2. `0002-redis-time-as-the-only-clock.md`: what goes wrong when instance clocks differ by 300 ms?
   Why does the script still accept an optional `now_ms`?
3. `0003-hash-tags-in-limiter-keys.md`: what is `CROSSSLOT`, and how does `rg:{acme}:tb:export`
   avoid it? What must tenant ids and resources never contain?
4. `0004-fail-closed-when-redis-is-unavailable.md`: fail open vs fail closed vs a local fallback. Who
   pays for each choice?
5. `0005-hashed-api-keys-and-constant-time-admin-token.md`: clear text vs bcrypt vs SHA-256 of a
   128-bit random key. Why is a fast hash fine here when it is wrong for passwords?

Each ADR is one page: context, options with pros/cons, decision, consequences.

steps.title: Write the Lua scripts → `spec/lua/`
steps.content_md:
Read `spec/lua/README.md`: it fixes the calling convention every track will use (`KEYS[1]` limiter
state, `KEYS[2]` usage ring, `ARGV` limit, window_ms, cost and an optional `now_ms`; the result
`{allowed, remaining, retry_after_ms, reset_after_ms}`). Each script must read, decide and write in
one call, use `redis.call('TIME')` unless `now_ms` is given, set a TTL on every key it writes, and
count the request in a ring of 180 one-minute slots (`m<slot>`, `a<slot>`, `d<slot>` with
`slot = minute % 180`).

Run them by hand with fixed clocks (database 9, so nothing else is touched):
```bash
R="docker compose exec -T redis redis-cli -n 9"
for t in 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 1000 13000; do
  $R EVAL "$(cat spec/lua/token_bucket.lua)" 2 'rg:{demo}:tb:default' 'rg:{demo}:usage' 5 60000 1 $t | tr '\n' ' '; echo
done
# 1 4 0 12000 / 1 3 0 24000 / 1 2 0 36000 / 1 1 0 48000 / 1 0 0 60000
# 0 0 12000 60000      <- the 6th request: denied, retry in 12 s (one token per 60000/5 ms)
# 1 0 0 60000          <- 12 s later one token has refilled
for t in 59000 59000 59000 61000 75000 80000; do
  $R EVAL "$(cat spec/lua/sliding_window.lua)" 2 'rg:{demo}:sw:default' 'rg:{demo}:usage' 3 60000 1 $t | tr '\n' ' '; echo
done
# three allowed at 0:59, then at 1:01: "0 0 19000 …" (denied; a fixed window would allow it)
$R TTL 'rg:{demo}:tb:default'; $R HGETALL 'rg:{demo}:usage'; $R FLUSHDB
```
If your numbers differ, find out which of you is right by doing the maths on paper. The same
sequences become integration tests in Phase 4, against your pure functions.

steps.title: Map the contract
steps.content_md:
For every path in `spec/openapi.yaml`, write the FR number next to it (a table in `architecture.md`).
Any endpoint without a requirement, or any requirement without an endpoint, is a design bug: fix one of
the two. Check that every admin path declares `security: [admin]` and the tenant paths
`security: [apiKey]`, and that `/health` declares none. Validate the file:
```bash
pipx run openapi-spec-validator spec/openapi.yaml       # or: npx @redocly/cli lint spec/openapi.yaml
```

git commit -m "docs(spec): architecture, ADRs 0001-0005, Lua scripts"

Reject suggestions that call `KEYS`, that move the clock into the app, or that use floats in the sliding window (three languages round floats differently).

closed with 503. Then list when failing open is genuinely the better choice. Keep it under 250 words.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking each claim against your ADR-0004 (who is harmed in each case, how long outages last, what an abusive tenant does during one) and recording the strongest counter-argument in the ADR's *Consequences*. A good ADR admits what the rejected option does better; you will come back to this one in Phase 7.

quiz.q: Why is a Lua script safe when `GET` + decide in the app + `SET` is not?
options: Lua is faster than Java, Python or TypeScript
Redis runs the whole script without running any other command in between, so two instances cannot both see "1 token left"
Redis caches the GET
Scripts use a distributed lock internally
quiz.explanation: With read-decide-write, two requests can read 1 at the same time and both write 0. Inside a script the read and the write are one atomic step, and the second caller sees 0 and is denied.

quiz.q: A limit of 3 per 60 s, fixed window. Requests at 0:59 (×3) and 1:00 (×3). How many are allowed?
quiz.explanation: A fixed window resets at 1:00, so 6 requests pass within one second: twice the limit. The sliding window counter weights the previous window and denies the second burst.

quiz.q: Why do the scripts read `redis.call('TIME')` instead of receiving the time from the app?
options: Lua has no clock
App instances' clocks drift; one clock in Redis makes every instance agree about "now"
TIME is more precise than the app clock
Redis Cluster requires it
quiz.explanation: If instance A is 300 ms ahead of instance B, B can "un-refill" a bucket A just refilled. `now_ms` exists only so tests are deterministic (ADR-0002).

quiz.q: Why are the limiter keys named `rg:{acme}:tb:export` with braces?
options: Braces make keys sort first
In Redis Cluster only the part in braces is hashed, so all keys a script touches for one tenant land in the same slot
Braces are required for hash-type keys
To hide the tenant id
quiz.explanation: A script may only touch keys of one slot; without the hash tag the bucket and the usage ring could be on different nodes and the call would fail with `CROSSSLOT` (ADR-0003).

quiz.q: Why is SHA-256 acceptable for API keys when it is wrong for passwords?
options: SHA-256 is slower than bcrypt
The keys are 128 random bits, so there is no dictionary or brute force to slow down, and a fast hash keeps every check cheap
API keys are not secrets
Redis cannot store bcrypt hashes
quiz.explanation: Passwords are short and guessable, so they need a slow hash. A random 128-bit key cannot be guessed at any speed; what matters is that a leaked Redis dump does not contain usable keys (ADR-0005).

quiz.q: Redis freezes for 30 seconds. What does v1.0 answer for a check?
options: `200` with `allowed: true`
`429` with `Retry-After`
`503 limiter-unavailable` with `Retry-After: 1`, after the 1 s command timeout
Nothing: the request hangs until Redis is back
quiz.explanation: ADR-0004 chooses to fail closed: the protection never disappears silently. Phase 7 measures what this costs in a game day and refines it.

Atomicity with Redis Lua scripts, and why one shared clock matters in a distributed system.
Key design for Redis Cluster (hash tags), TTLs everywhere, and input validation as a key-safety measure.

phases.heading: Phase 3 · Implementation in five milestones
phases.why_md:
This is where a limiter either keeps its promises or quietly lets traffic through. The tests are
already written: they describe every rule from Phase 1 (the exact token-bucket and sliding-window
maths, the headers, `Retry-After`, costs, resets, usage) and every refusal (no token, a rotated key,
a deleted tenant, a cost above the limit, a tenant id with a `*`). Working test-first, one milestone
at a time, keeps you honest and gives you a green bar to show for each step. It is also where AI
assistants are most tempting and most dangerous: they write a plausible limiter fast, and the bugs
they leave (a `GET` then `SET` around Redis, a float that rounds differently in each language, a
token compared with `==`, `KEYS rg:*` in a reset) only show up under real load.
objectives: Implement RateGuard in **your** track in five milestones: **M1** validation + security (API keys, admin token) · **M2** the two algorithms as pure functions · **M3** the Redis key layout and the Redis store (your Lua scripts) · **M4** tenants, the limiter service and the HTTP API · **M5** usage statistics and the AI policy advisor.
Use the pending list to work test-first.
Keep the HTTP layer thin and the business logic in framework-free services with an injected clock.

steps.title: M2: the algorithms as pure functions (FR-7, FR-8)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **token-bucket**, **sliding-window** and **memory-store**. Each algorithm is one function:
`(state or null, limit, window_ms, cost, now) → (new state, decision)`. No Redis, no clock, no I/O,
which makes them perfect for test-first work. They are the same maths as your Lua scripts from
Phase 2, line by line:
* **Token bucket:** a new bucket starts full; refill `(now - ts) × limit / window_ms`, capped at
  `limit`, only when `now > ts` (a clock that goes backwards refills nothing); allowed when
  `tokens ≥ cost`. `retryAfterMs = ceil((cost - tokens) × window_ms / limit)`,
  `resetAfterMs = ceil((limit - tokens) × window_ms / limit)`, `remaining = floor(tokens)`.
* **Sliding window counter:** window index `now // window_ms`; move `cur` to `prev` when one window
  has passed, drop both after two; then, **in integers**,
  `weighted = prev × (window_ms - elapsed) + cur × window_ms` and allow when
  `weighted + cost × window_ms ≤ limit × window_ms`. The tests pin down the two `retryAfterMs` cases
  (fits once the old window slides out / only fits in the next window).

The in-memory store calls these functions, so once they are green, every API test that follows runs
on your maths. Compare your numbers with Step 2.4 of Phase 2: they must be identical.

steps.title: M3: Redis keys and the Redis store (FR-12, FR-13, ADR-0001 … 0003)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **keys**. `keys` builds every Redis key in one place: `rg:tenants`, `rg:tenant:<id>`,
`rg:key:<hash>`, `rg:{<id>}:tb:<resource>`, `rg:{<id>}:sw:<resource>`, `rg:{<id>}:usage`, the
`SCAN` pattern `rg:{<id>}:*` and the usage slot (`minute % 180`).

Then the **Redis store** (no unit tests: the integration tests in Phase 4 cover it, and your `curl`
session in M4 is the first check). The in-memory store is your specification:
1. **Load the Lua scripts** from `LUA_DIR` at start-up and call them by SHA (`EVALSHA`); reload on
   `NOSCRIPT` (your client library may do this for you: find out how).
2. `check` passes `KEYS` = limiter key + usage key and `ARGV` = limit, window_ms, cost (+ `now_ms` only
   when a test gives one) and maps the reply `[allowed, remaining, retryAfterMs, resetAfterMs]`.
3. `create_tenant` decides races with `SADD rg:tenants <id>` (`0` = someone else won → duplicate),
   then writes the hash and the key lookup in one `MULTI`/`EXEC`.
4. `save_tenant` (policy change, rotation) and `delete_tenant` use `MULTI`/`EXEC`; rotation deletes the
   old `rg:key:<hash>` in the same transaction.
5. `reset` and `delete` find limiter keys with **`SCAN MATCH rg:{<id>}:*`**, never `KEYS` (it blocks
   Redis for everyone while it walks the whole key space).
6. Every Redis error and timeout becomes `StoreUnavailable` → `503 limiter-unavailable`.

steps.title: M4: tenants, the limiter and the API (FR-1 … FR-12, FR-15, FR-16)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **tenants**, **limiter**, **api-admin** and **api-limits**.
* `TenantService`: create (new key, hash, prefix, `409` on duplicate), list, get (`404`), set_policy,
  rotate_key, delete, reset and `authenticate(X-API-Key)`: format check, hash, look up, `401
  invalid-api-key` for anything that fails. The plain key leaves the service only in the create and
  rotate results.
* `LimiterService`: validate `{resource?, cost?}`, refuse `cost > limit` with `422` (it could never
  pass, and the client would retry forever), call the store, and build the headers:
  `X-RateLimit-Reset` and `Retry-After` are whole seconds **rounded up** (`Retry-After: 0` would make
  clients retry at once). `enforce` turns a denial into `429 rate-limited` for the demo endpoint.

```bash
docker compose up -d redis && make run      # in tracks/<track>
ADMIN='Authorization: Bearer local-admin-token-change-me-0123456789abcdef'
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/tenants -H "$ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"id":"acme","name":"Acme Corp","policy":{"algorithm":"TOKEN_BUCKET","limit":5,"windowSeconds":60}}'
# 201 ... "apiKey":"rg_…"   <- shown once; copy it
KEY=rg_paste_it_here
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} ' localhost:8080/api/v1/demo/hello -H "X-API-Key: $KEY"; done
# 200 200 200 200 200 429
curl -si -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/limits/check -H "X-API-Key: $KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
docker compose exec redis redis-cli --scan --pattern 'rg:*'    # look at your keys; note the {acme} tag
docker compose exec redis redis-cli HGETALL 'rg:{acme}:tb:demo'
```
Now start a **second instance** on port 8081 (`PORT=8081 make run` in another terminal) and repeat the
loop half on each port after a reset (`POST /admin/tenants/acme/reset`): still five `200`s in total.
That is NFR-1 working.

steps.title: M5: usage statistics and the AI policy advisor (FR-13, FR-14, NFR-7)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **advisor** and **api-advice**. Three pieces:
1. **Usage statistics** (`summarize`): total, allowed, denied, denied percent (integer, rounded down),
   active minutes, peak minute and its denials, median and 90th percentile (nearest rank) of the
   minutes that had traffic, and the capacity per minute of the policy (`limit × 60 / windowSeconds`). The tests fix every definition (median of an even count,
   percentile index), because the advisor's texts quote these numbers.
2. **The rule advisor**: five rules in a fixed order: no traffic → `KEEP`; a spike (peak ≥ 5 × median,
   most denials in that minute) → `INVESTIGATE` (a retry storm or abuse is not growth); ≥ 10 % denied →
   `RAISE_LIMIT` to the 90th percentile + 20 %, at most × 10; far below capacity for 10+ minutes →
   `LOWER_LIMIT` to twice the peak; otherwise `KEEP`. The summary texts are checked word for word.
3. **The LLM advisor**: send only the policy and the statistics (numbers, never keys or names) and ask
   for **only** a JSON object. `parse_advice` validates the answer **like untrusted user input**: strip
   a Markdown fence, known action only, a limit for the limit actions only, a raise above the current
   limit and at most × 10, a lower below it, a summary of at most 400 characters. Any failure throws,
   and `AdvisorService` falls back to the rules with `fallback: true`. Advice is returned, never applied.

```bash
curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/tenants/acme/advice -H "$ADMIN"
curl -s 'localhost:8080/api/v1/admin/tenants/acme/usage?minutes=5' -H "$ADMIN"
```
Optional, with a local model: `docker compose --profile ollama up -d`, pull `llama3.2:1b`, run your track
with `AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1` and compare the answers. Then stop Ollama
and call it again: `provider` becomes `rules` and `fallback` `true`, with a `200`.

steps.title: Review the AI's code (exercise)
steps.content_md:
An assistant produced this "simpler" token bucket for the Redis store (pseudo-code). Find the bugs
**before** reading on, then point to the test that catches them.
```text
state = redis.hgetall("bucket:" + tenantId + ":" + resource)
tokens = min(limit, state.tokens + (System.now() - state.ts) / 1000.0 * (limit / windowSeconds))
if tokens >= cost:
    redis.hset("bucket:" + tenantId + ":" + resource, {tokens: tokens - cost, ts: System.now()})
    return ALLOWED
return DENIED
```
Four bugs: read-decide-write from the app is **not atomic** (two instances both spend the last token);
the **app clock** is used (drift between instances); `limit / windowSeconds` is **integer division**
in Java when both are `int` (5 / 60 = 0: the bucket never refills); and the key
has **no hash tag and no TTL**, and a resource containing `:` collides with another tenant's key. The
unit tests *"refills continuously"* fail against the maths, and in Phase 4 the integration test
*"concurrent checks never exceed the limit"* shows the race. Note in `AI_LOG.md` how you found it.

quiz.q: Why do the algorithm functions take `now` as a parameter instead of reading the clock?
options: It is faster than the system clock
Tests can replay exact timelines (refill after 12 s, a clock going backwards) without sleeping, and the same function serves Lua parity tests and the in-memory store
Redis requires it
To support time zones
quiz.explanation: Pure functions are deterministic: same inputs, same output. Code that calls `now()` inside can only be tested by waiting.

quiz.q: Why is `cost > limit` a `422` instead of a normal denial?
options: Redis cannot store large numbers
Such a request can never pass, so a denial with a `Retry-After` would make a well-behaved client retry forever
Costs above the limit are a security attack
The contract does not allow `allowed: false`
quiz.explanation: A denial says "later". A request that can never succeed needs a different, permanent answer the client can act on.

quiz.q: Why compare the admin token with `hmac.compare_digest` / `MessageDigest.isEqual` / `timingSafeEqual` instead of `==`?
options: It is shorter to write
`==` stops at the first different character, so response times reveal how much of a guessed token was right
`==` does not work on long strings
The constant-time functions also check the `Bearer` prefix
quiz.explanation: Timing attacks recover a secret value byte by byte. Constant-time comparison removes the signal.

quiz.q: Why does `reset` use `SCAN MATCH rg:{acme}:*` instead of `KEYS rg:{acme}:*`?
options: `KEYS` does not support patterns
`KEYS` walks the whole key space in one blocking command, stalling every other client; `SCAN` walks it in small steps
`SCAN` is atomic
`KEYS` cannot read hash tags
quiz.explanation: Redis is single-threaded: one slow command delays every limiter check of every tenant. `SCAN` trades a few round trips for never blocking.

quiz.q: `Retry-After` for a `retryAfterMs` of 1 200 ms. What is the header?
quiz.explanation: Whole seconds, rounded **up**. A client that waits 1 s retries too early and is denied again; `0` would mean "retry now".

quiz.q: What must `POST /admin/tenants/{id}/advice` do when the LLM endpoint is unreachable?
options: Return `502 Bad Gateway`
Return `KEEP` without explanation
Answer with the rule advisor, `200`, `provider: "rules"` and `fallback: true`
Return `503` until the LLM is back
quiz.explanation: The AI is an optional layer on a deterministic baseline (NFR-7). Admins always get advice, and `fallback` makes the degradation visible.

quiz.q: In the AI-generated token bucket, which bug lets two instances admit more than the limit even with perfect single-instance tests?
options: The missing TTL
Reading the bucket and writing it back in separate commands from the app
Using `HGETALL`
Returning `DENIED` without a retry time
quiz.explanation: Two instances both read 1 token and both write 0. Only an atomic script (or a transaction that retries) closes the race; the Lua script does it in one round trip.

phases.heading: Phase 4 · Testing: Lua parity, concurrency across instances, security, coverage gate
phases.why_md:
Unit tests with an in-memory store prove your maths. They cannot prove that your Lua scripts do the
**same** maths, that a check is really atomic when forty requests arrive at once from two app
instances, that keys expire, that a reset touches one tenant only, or that the store survives a
`SCRIPT FLUSH`. Integration tests against a **real** Redis do. A load test then shows the property
the whole project exists for: however requests are spread over instances, exactly `limit` pass. A
coverage gate stops the suite from quietly rotting. Together they let you change code (or accept an
AI's refactor) without fear, which is exactly what you need before CI in Phase 5.

Run the integration suite against the Compose Redis using a **separate** database (15).
Prove that the Lua scripts and the pure functions agree step by step, and that parallel checks never exceed the limit, from one and from two app instances.
Run the load test against two instances and read its latency numbers.
Enforce ≥ 85 % line coverage locally and understand what the number does and does not mean.

steps.title: Read the parity, concurrency and security tests
steps.content_md:
Open the integration file and find these cases. Each maps to a requirement or an ADR:
- **the Lua script and the pure function agree step by step** (ADR-0001), for both algorithms: the
  same sequence of `(now, cost)` pairs, with a fixed `now_ms`, must give identical decisions.
- **concurrent checks never exceed the limit** (NFR-1): many threads / promises check at once against a
  small limit; exactly `limit` are allowed.
- **two app instances share one limit** (NFR-1): two store objects (two "instances") on one Redis.
- **exactly one of several racing creates wins** (FR-2): `SADD` decides, the rest get a duplicate.
- **every key has a TTL and usage is recorded** (NFR-6, FR-13), **the usage ring reads the current
  minutes** (FR-13).
- **reset forgets one tenant only** (FR-12, ADR-0003).
- **the Redis clock is used without an override** (ADR-0002).
- **scripts are reloaded after `SCRIPT FLUSH`** (failover, restart without persistence).
- **an unreachable Redis is a store-unavailable error** (NFR-4) and **the whole API runs on Redis**,
  including parallel HTTP requests against the demo endpoint.

steps.content_md:
A test you have never seen fail proves nothing. Pick the concurrency test and break the code on
purpose in a scratch branch: replace the `EVALSHA` in your store's `check` with "read the hash, call
your pure function in the app, write the hash back". Run `make test-integration` (repeat a few times if
needed): it must go red, for the right reason (more allowed than the limit). Restore it. Then change
one line of `token_bucket.lua` (for example drop the `math.min` cap) and watch the parity test fail.

quiz.q: Which bug can ONLY an integration test catch here?
options: A wrong error message for a too-long tenant name
A typo in `sliding_window.lua` that makes it disagree with the pure function at a window boundary
A wrong rounding of `Retry-After`
A missing admin-token check in an endpoint
quiz.explanation: Unit tests use the in-memory store, which calls the pure functions; the Lua never runs there. The other bugs live in code the unit tests already exercise.

quiz.q: Why does the parity test pass a fixed `now_ms` to the script?
options: Redis `TIME` is not precise enough
So the script and the pure function see exactly the same timeline and any difference is a maths bug, not timing noise
Production also passes `now_ms`
Lua cannot read the clock in tests
quiz.explanation: Determinism makes failures meaningful. A separate test checks that, without the override, the script really uses the Redis clock.

quiz.q: Why does the concurrency test need real parallel requests?
options: Sequential requests are too slow
Over-admission only appears when two checks read the same state before either writes
Redis rejects sequential requests
To test the connection pool size
quiz.explanation: Sequentially, the second check already sees the lower token count. Atomic execution of the script is what makes the parallel case safe, and only a parallel test shows it.

quiz.q: Your coverage is 93 %. What does that prove?
options: The code has no concurrency bugs
All requirements are implemented
93 % of lines executed during the tests. It says nothing about whether the assertions are meaningful
The integration tests are not needed
quiz.explanation: Coverage finds *untested* code; it cannot find *wrong* tests. Use it as a floor, not a target.

quiz.q: Why must `TEST_REDIS_URL` never point at a Redis you do not own?
options: The tests would be slower
The tests run `FLUSHDB` on database 15 before every test, deleting whatever someone else stored there
Redis allows only one client
The tests change the Redis configuration
quiz.explanation: Destructive test setup is fine on an isolated database and an incident anywhere else. Check the port before you run the suite on a machine with other projects.

quiz.q: Why break the code on purpose and watch a test fail?
options: To practise git
A test that cannot fail gives false confidence; seeing it go red proves it checks the behaviour
The coverage tool requires it
To make CI slower
quiz.explanation: It is a cheap form of mutation testing. Assistants often write tests that pass against any implementation.

phases.title: CI with GitHub Actions
phases.heading: Phase 5 · Continuous integration with GitHub Actions
phases.why_md:
"It passed on my machine" is not evidence. CI runs the same checks on a clean machine for every push
and pull request, so a broken change never reaches `main`. It is also the cheapest code reviewer you
will ever have. In this phase you grow the starter workflow into a real pipeline: path filters, a
reusable workflow, service containers for integration tests, caching, a coverage artefact and one
required status check.

Every keyword used here is explained slowly in **[docs/github-actions-explained.md](github-actions-explained.md)**.
Read it side by side with the YAML.
objectives: Explain triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, matrices, caching and artefacts.
Write a **reusable workflow** (`workflow_call`) that runs one track's full check, and call it three times.
Run integration tests in CI with a Redis **service container**.
Skip unaffected tracks with a **path filter**, and still have a single required check (`ci-ok`).
Validate the OpenAPI contract in CI and enable **Dependabot**.
Protect `main` so a PR cannot be merged while CI is red.

steps.title: Read the starter workflow
steps.content_md:
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It is a **matrix** over `[java, python, typescript]`; each matrix job
sets up one toolchain (`if: matrix.track == 'java'`), then runs `make install`, `make lint` and `make test`.
The same Makefile targets exist in every track, so CI does not need three different scripts.

steps.title: Create the reusable workflow
steps.content_md:
Create `.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml` with `on: workflow_call` and an input `track`. Give its job:
- `services:` `redis:7.4-alpine` with a health check (`redis-cli ping`) and a published port,
- `env:` `TEST_REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379/15` (the tests flush database 15 before each test),
- the setup steps from the starter, then `make install lint test`,
- `make coverage` (unit + integration + the 85 % gate),
- `actions/upload-artifact@v4` for the coverage report (`if: always()`).

steps.title: Rewrite `ci.yml` as an orchestrator
steps.content_md:
1. A `changes` job with `dorny/paths-filter@v3` that outputs `docs`, `shared`, `java`, `python`, `typescript`.
2. A `contract` job (only when shared files or docs change): `pipx run openapi-spec-validator spec/openapi.yaml`,
   `shellcheck` on `scripts/*.sh` and `python3 scripts/build-cms.py --check` (the course export must match `docs/`).
3. Three jobs `java`, `python`, `typescript`, each `uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml`
   with `if:` on its path output.
4. A final `ci-ok` job with `if: always()` and `needs:` on all of them that fails when any result is
   `failure` or `cancelled`. Skipped is fine.

The reference is at `git show phase-5-end:.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

steps.title: Lint your workflows before pushing
steps.content_md:
```bash
# https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint  (Go binary; also available via Homebrew / Docker)
go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest
actionlint                       # run from the repo root
```
`actionlint` catches typos in expressions, unknown inputs, bad `needs` and shell bugs (via shellcheck)
before GitHub ever sees them.

steps.title: Dependabot
steps.content_md:
Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with one entry per ecosystem: `maven` in `/tracks/java`, `pip` in
`/tracks/python`, `npm` in `/tracks/typescript`, and `github-actions` in `/`. Group minor + patch updates
so you get one PR per ecosystem per week.

steps.title: Protect `main`
steps.content_md:
In your fork: **Settings → Branches → Add branch ruleset** (or classic rule) for `main`:
- Require a pull request before merging.
- Require status checks to pass → add **`ci-ok`** (it appears after the first run).
- Block force pushes.

Because skipped jobs count as success, a docs-only PR still gets a green `ci-ok` quickly.

steps.title: Prove it works
steps.content_md:
Open a PR that breaks one test in **one** track: only that track's job runs (path filter) and `ci-ok`
goes red, so the merge button is blocked. Fix it and watch it go green. Then open a PR that only touches
`spec/openapi.yaml`: all jobs run, because a contract change affects every track.

quiz.q: What does `on: workflow_call` mean?
options: The workflow runs when someone calls the repository's API
The workflow can be used as a reusable workflow by other workflows (`jobs.<id>.uses`)
The workflow runs on every push
The workflow can only be run manually
quiz.explanation: A reusable workflow is like a function: it declares `inputs`, and the caller passes them with `with:`.

quiz.q: Why is `ci-ok` the only required check instead of every job?
options: GitHub allows only one required check
With path filters some jobs are skipped; one aggregator job gives a stable name that is green when nothing failed
It makes CI faster
Reusable workflows cannot be required checks
quiz.explanation: Required checks are matched by name. An aggregator with `if: always()` survives jobs being skipped or renamed.

quiz.q: How do integration tests reach Redis in CI?
options: They use the in-memory store
They connect to a free cloud Redis
A `services:` container runs next to the job and its port is published on `localhost`
Docker Compose is started inside the test
quiz.explanation: Service containers live for one job, are health-checked before steps start, and are thrown away afterwards.

quiz.q: What does `cache: npm` (or `maven`/`pip`) in a setup action do?
options: Caches the build output
Restores the package download cache keyed by a hash of the lock file, so installs are faster
Commits `node_modules` to the repo
Skips the install step
quiz.explanation: The key changes when `package-lock.json` / `pom.xml` / `requirements-dev.txt` changes, so you never get stale dependencies.

quiz.q: Which default `permissions` block is safest for a CI workflow that only reads code?
options: `permissions: write-all`
`permissions: contents: read`
No block at all
`permissions: packages: write`
quiz.explanation: Least privilege. Jobs that need more (e.g. pushing images) ask for it explicitly, as `deploy.yml` does in Phase 6.

recap: Workflow anatomy: triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, `defaults`, `concurrency`.
Reusable workflows with inputs, and an orchestrator workflow that calls them.
Service containers for real integration tests in CI.
Path filters plus an aggregator job for fast and safe required checks.
Caching, artefacts, actionlint, Dependabot and branch protection.

phases.title: Containerise, deliver, and (optionally) deploy to a free tier
phases.heading: Phase 6 · Containerise, deliver and (optionally) deploy
phases.why_md:
A container image is the unit you actually ship: the same bytes run on your laptop, in CI and in
the cloud. In this phase you write a production-grade Dockerfile, run the whole stack with one
command, prove it with a black-box smoke test, run **two instances of your track against one Redis**
the way it would run in production, and publish versioned images to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR)
automatically on every release tag. Deploying to the cloud is **optional**: everything graded in this
phase works offline on your laptop.
objectives: Write a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile with a `HEALTHCHECK` for your track that ships the shared Lua scripts.
Add your app to `docker-compose.yml` as a profile and start the stack with `docker compose --profile <track> up`.
Run the language-agnostic smoke test against your container (and against the other tracks' images).
Run two instances behind one Redis (`pair` profile) and repeat the load test.
Add a Docker build + smoke job to CI.
Write `deploy.yml`: on a `v*.*.*` tag, build and push images to GHCR; optionally trigger a Render deploy that is **skipped gracefully** when no secret is configured.
Cut release **v1.0.0** with a CHANGELOG entry.

steps.title: The Dockerfile (build context = repository root)
steps.content_md:
All tracks copy the shared Lua scripts into the image, so the build context is the repo root and the
Dockerfile lives in the track: `docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile .`. Rules:
- **Multi-stage:** compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage.
- **Dependencies before source:** copy the manifest, install, then copy `src`, so code changes reuse the dependency layer.
- **Non-root user**, `EXPOSE 8080`, `HEALTHCHECK` hitting `/health`, `COPY spec/lua ./lua` and `LUA_DIR=/app/lua`.

<!-- track:java -->
```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/java/pom.xml tracks/java/checkstyle.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY tracks/java/src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests -Dcheckstyle.skip -Djacoco.skip=true \
    && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination /extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
ENV PORT=8080 LUA_DIR=/app/lua JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
WORKDIR /app
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home app
COPY --from=build /extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/application/ ./
COPY spec/lua ./lua
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health > /dev/null || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]

steps.title: Compose profiles: one command for the whole stack
steps.content_md:
Add a service per track to `docker-compose.yml` under a **profile**, sharing one block of environment
variables (a YAML anchor `x-app-env`), `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, and port
`${APP_PORT:-8080}:8080`. Inside Compose the app reaches Redis as `redis://redis:6379/0`, not
`localhost`. The Compose file sets a **local-only** `ADMIN_TOKEN` through `${VAR:-default}`, so
`docker compose up` works out of the box. A real deployment sets its own value: the default is
public, in this repository. Redis runs with `--appendonly yes`, so tenants and keys survive a restart.
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

steps.title: Smoke test (the same for every track)
steps.content_md:
```bash
scripts/smoke-test.sh                      # default http://localhost:8080
```
It checks 53 behaviours with only `bash`, `curl` and `xargs`: health, `404` and `401` as
`problem+json`, creating a token-bucket tenant (the key is shown once and never again), a duplicate
id (`409`), an id that could break a Redis key (`400`), a check with all `X-RateLimit-*` headers, a
cost above the limit (`422`), an unknown key (`401`), three allowed `hello`s and a `429` with
`Retry-After`, a sliding-window tenant whose denied check is still a `200` answer, **parallel**
checks against a limit of 5 (exactly 5 allowed), reset, key rotation (the old key dies at once), a
policy change, usage, advice, and deleting a tenant (its key is revoked). It creates its own uniquely
named tenants and deletes them at the end, so it is safe to run repeatedly. Against a deployment,
pass the admin token as `SMOKE_ADMIN_TOKEN`.

Because the contract and the scripts are shared, try another track's image against the same Redis:
`docker compose stop app-<yours>` and `docker compose --profile python up -d`. Same results. Also run
the AI fallback check:
```bash
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=1000 docker compose --profile <track> up -d --wait
EXPECT_FALLBACK=true scripts/smoke-test.sh      # the advice reports provider "rules" and fallback: true
```

steps.title: Two instances, one Redis
steps.content_md:
The `pair` profile starts two containers of the same image on ports 8081 and 8082:
```bash
TRACK=<track> docker compose --profile pair up -d --build --wait
python3 scripts/load-test.py                   # http://localhost:8081 and http://localhost:8082
```
`allowed` must equal the limit, exactly as in Phase 4, now with real containers and a real network.
Stop one of the two in the middle of a run (`docker compose stop app-b`): the other keeps enforcing
the same limit, because no instance holds any state.

steps.title: CI: build the image and smoke-test it
steps.content_md:
Add a `docker` job (matrix over tracks) to `ci.yml`: `docker/setup-buildx-action`,
`docker/build-push-action` with `load: true` and the GitHub Actions layer cache (`cache-from/to: type=gha`),
then `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --no-build --wait`, the smoke test, logs on failure and `down -v`.

steps.title: Continuous delivery to GHCR: `deploy.yml`
steps.content_md:
Trigger on `push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]`. The job needs `permissions: packages: write` and logs in to
`ghcr.io` with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`; no personal token required. Image names must be lower-case
(the org is `AICanCode-org`), so compute `ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/rateguard-<track>`.
`docker/metadata-action` turns tag `v1.0.0` into image tags `1.0.0`, `1.0`, `sha-<short>` and `latest`.
Read `docs/github-actions-explained.md` §9–§12 for every detail.

steps.title: Release v1.0.0
steps.content_md:
```bash
# update CHANGELOG.md: move "Unreleased" items under "## [1.0.0] - <date>"
git commit -am "chore(release): v1.0.0"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "RateGuard v1.0.0"
git push origin main --follow-tags
```
Watch **Actions → Deploy**: three images appear under your profile's **Packages**. New GHCR packages
are **private** by default. Make one public (Package settings → Change visibility) if a host should pull
it without credentials.

steps.title: OPTIONAL: deploy to a free tier
steps.content_md:
You do not need a cloud account to finish this course. If you want a public URL:

| Piece | Free option | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App | **Render** web service from an *existing image* (`ghcr.io/<you>/rateguard-<track>:latest`) | Free instances spin down after 15 minutes without traffic; the next request takes about a minute (cold start). |
| Redis | **Upstash** Redis free tier, or Render Key Value (free) | Use the TLS URL (`rediss://…`) as `REDIS_URL`. Free plans limit commands per day and memory, and some do not persist data: read the limits, and remember tenants live in Redis. |
| Secrets | Render env vars | Set your own `ADMIN_TOKEN` (`openssl rand -hex 32`). Never reuse the Compose default. |
| LLM | none (rules), or a free Gemini / Groq key | `AI_PROVIDER=llm`, `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` as Render env vars. Only usage numbers are sent, but say so in your README. |

Free-tier limits change. Check each provider's pricing page before you rely on it. Fly.io is **not**
used: at the time of writing it needs a payment method and bills usage, with no free tier for new accounts.

To let CI deploy for you:
1. Render → your service → **Settings → Deploy Hook**: copy the URL.
2. GitHub → **Settings → Environments → New environment `production`** (optionally add yourself as a
   required reviewer). Add the **secret** `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` and the **variables** `RENDER_APP_URL`
   (e.g. `https://rateguard-xyz.onrender.com`) and `DEPLOY_TRACK` (`java`, `python` or `typescript`).
   Optionally add the secret `SMOKE_ADMIN_TOKEN` (your live `ADMIN_TOKEN`) so the full smoke test runs
   against the live app; without it only `/health` is checked.
3. Push a tag. The `render` job calls the hook with `imgURL=` set to the exact version, waits for
   `/health`, and runs the smoke test against the live URL. Without the secret the job prints a notice
   and **succeeds**, so forks without cloud accounts stay green.

My container works locally but on Render /health times out for the first minute after idle, then works,

quiz.q: Why do the Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest before the source code?
options: Docker requires that order
So that the dependency layer is cached and only rebuilt when the manifest changes
To make the image smaller
To run tests faster
quiz.explanation: Layers are cached top-down; anything after a changed layer is rebuilt. Source changes often, dependencies rarely.

quiz.q: Inside Docker Compose, which `REDIS_URL` does the app use?
options: `redis://localhost:6379/0`
`redis://redis:6379/0` (the service name)
`redis://host.docker.internal:6379/0`
quiz.explanation: Each container has its own `localhost`. Compose gives services DNS names on a shared network.

quiz.q: Why does the build context have to be the repository root?
options: Docker cannot build from sub-folders
The image needs `spec/lua/` as well as the track's code, and a build can only copy files inside its context
To include the `.env` file
To speed up the build
quiz.explanation: The scripts are shared by all tracks, so they live outside `tracks/<track>`. `.dockerignore` keeps everything else (and `.env`) out of the context.

quiz.q: A fork has no `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` secret. What does the `render` job do on a tag push?
options: Fails the workflow
Deploys to a default account
Prints a notice and succeeds; the image is still pushed to the fork's GHCR
Waits for someone to add the secret
quiz.explanation: Optional infrastructure must not make the pipeline red. Secrets are read into `env:` and tested with `if: env.X == ''`.

quiz.q: You stop one of the two `pair` instances during a load test. What happens to the limit?
options: It doubles, because the other instance forgets the shared state
It halves
Nothing: all state is in Redis, so the remaining instance enforces exactly the same limit
Requests fail until both are back
quiz.explanation: Stateless app instances can come and go (deploys, crashes, autoscaling) without changing any decision.

quiz.q: Why must a deployment never use the `ADMIN_TOKEN` from `docker-compose.yml`?
options: It is too short
It is public in the repository, so anyone could create tenants, read usage and reset limits on your service
Render rejects it
It expires after 30 days
quiz.explanation: Defaults are for laptops; deployments get their own token from the host's environment variables.

recap: Production Dockerfiles: multi-stage, layer caching, non-root, health checks, `.dockerignore`, shared files in the image.
Compose profiles to run any track, or two instances of one, against the same Redis with one command.
Black-box smoke tests that work for any implementation of a contract.
Image builds with layer caching in CI, and delivery to GHCR with the built-in token on version tags.
Optional, secret-gated deployment that degrades gracefully, plus free-tier trade-offs (cold starts, Redis limits).
Semantic versioning and a CHANGELOG-driven release.

phases.title: Observability, game day and resilience
phases.heading: Phase 7 · Observability, game day and resilience (v1.1.0)
phases.why_md:
Shipping v1.0.0 is the start, not the end. In production you have to answer "is it working right now,
and if not, why?" without attaching a debugger. That needs three things: **logs** you can search,
**metrics** you can graph, and a **request ID** that ties a tenant's complaint ("we got 503s at 19:42")
to log lines. RateGuard sits in front of other people's traffic and depends on one thing it does not
control, Redis, so you will run a **game day** where Redis freezes, measure what tenants feel, and
discover that "fail closed" (ADR-0004) hurts more than the ADR predicted. You fix it with a **circuit
breaker** and your first **maintenance change**, driven by what tenants told you: a per-tenant
`failMode`, released backward compatibly as v1.1.0.
objectives: Give every request an `X-Request-ID` (reuse a safe incoming one, or generate a UUID) and put it in every log line.
Emit structured **JSON logs**: one object per line, one access-log line per request.
Expose `/metrics` in Prometheus text format with eight counters that are identical in every track.
Run a **game day**: freeze Redis with `docker pause`, measure checks and `/health`, write a short blameless post-mortem.
Add a Redis **circuit breaker** (3 failures in a row → open for `REDIS_BREAKER_COOLDOWN_MS` → one half-open trial) and reuse it for the LLM.
Ship a backward-compatible change: `policy.failMode` (`CLOSED` | `OPEN` | `LOCAL`), degraded decisions, `/health` `DEGRADED`, OpenAPI 1.1.0, ADR-0006, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
Review and merge one Dependabot PR.

steps.title: Request IDs
steps.content_md:
Rule (shared by all tracks): if the incoming `X-Request-ID` matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, echo it;
otherwise generate a UUID. Never echo arbitrary input: a header containing a newline could inject
fake log lines or headers.

<!-- track:java -->
A `OncePerRequestFilter` (`web/RequestIdFilter.java`) sets the response header, puts `requestId` in
the SLF4J **MDC** (so every log line in that request carries it) and logs one `rateguard.access` line
with `method`, `path`, `status` and `durationMs` using the fluent API
`LOG.atInfo().addKeyValue("status", …).log()`. `@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` makes it the first
filter, so even a `401` or a `404` gets an ID.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A Starlette middleware (`app/observability.py`) stores the ID in `request.state`, sets the response
header and logs one `rateguard.access` record with `extra={"fields": {...}}`. The middleware wraps the
whole app, so error responses (`400`, `401`, `404`, `503`) carry the header too.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Fastify has request IDs built in: `genReqId` (calling `incomingOrNewId()` from `src/observability.ts`)
with `requestIdHeader: false`, so we validate the incoming value ourselves, and a `LogController` with `requestIdLogLabel: "requestId"`.
An `onSend` hook copies `request.id` into the `X-Request-ID` response header.
<!-- /track -->

steps.title: `/metrics`
steps.content_md:
Eight counters, same names in all tracks (see `GET /metrics` in `spec/openapi.yaml`):

| Counter | Incremented when |
|---|---|
| `rateguard_decisions_allowed_total` | a check was allowed |
| `rateguard_decisions_denied_total` | a check was denied (a spike here is a tenant hitting its limit) |
| `rateguard_degraded_decisions_total` | a check was decided by the tenant's `failMode` because Redis was unavailable (Step 7.6) |
| `rateguard_store_errors_total` | a Redis call failed (refused, timed out, broken connection) |
| `rateguard_store_short_circuits_total` | the circuit breaker skipped a Redis call (Step 7.5) |
| `rateguard_tenants_created_total` | `POST /admin/tenants` created a tenant |
| `rateguard_ai_fallback_total` | an advice request fell back to the offline rules |
| `rateguard_llm_short_circuits_total` | the circuit breaker skipped an LLM call |

They are hand-rolled on purpose: the Prometheus text format is just
```text
# HELP rateguard_store_errors_total Redis calls that failed (refused, timed out, broken connection).
# TYPE rateguard_store_errors_total counter
rateguard_store_errors_total 3
```
In a bigger service you would use Micrometer (Java), `prometheus-client` (Python) or `prom-client` (Node).
`/metrics` is public in this course project; in production you would restrict it to the scraper's network.

steps.title: Game day: Redis freezes
steps.content_md:
A dead Redis is easy: the connection is refused and the error comes back in a millisecond. A
**frozen** Redis is worse: the kernel still accepts connections, but nothing answers, so every command
waits for the full `REDIS_TIMEOUT_MS` (1 s). That is what a Redis stuck in a slow command, a full disk,
a long fork for a snapshot or a network partition looks like. `docker pause` produces exactly that.
1. Start the stack at v1.0.0: `git switch --detach v1.0.0`, `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait`.
2. Get the script from the reference: `git show phase-7-end:scripts/game-day.sh > /tmp/game-day.sh && chmod +x /tmp/game-day.sh`,
   then `/tmp/game-day.sh <track>`. It creates three tenants with a limit of 5 per 60 s and the fail
   modes `CLOSED`, `OPEN` and `LOCAL` (v1.0 ignores the field: every tenant is effectively `CLOSED`),
   then runs phases of 10 requests per tenant: **baseline**, Redis **frozen**, `/health` while 40
   requests are in flight, Redis **back** immediately, and Redis back **after 6 s**.
3. Write down for each phase: status codes, average and maximum latency, how many decisions were
   degraded, `/health`'s status and latency, the warnings in the logs, and (from v1.1) the counters.
   What did tenants get? What did the load balancer get from `/health`, and what would it do with it?
4. Write `docs/postmortem-<date>-redis-freeze.md`: summary, impact, timeline, root cause, what went
   well, what to improve, action items. Blameless: describe systems, not people. Read the reference
   post-mortem **after** writing yours (`git show phase-7-end:docs/postmortem-2026-10-02-redis-freeze.md`).

steps.title: Fix: a circuit breaker in front of Redis
steps.content_md:
Wrap the store in a `GuardedStore` that sends every call through a `CircuitBreaker`:
- **CLOSED:** calls go through. 3 store failures **in a row** open the circuit.
- **OPEN:** calls fail immediately with "store unavailable" for `REDIS_BREAKER_COOLDOWN_MS` (5 s), and
  `rateguard_store_short_circuits_total` is incremented. No request waits for a timeout any more.
- **HALF-OPEN:** after the cooldown, exactly **one** trial call goes through. Success closes the circuit;
  failure re-opens it for another cooldown.

Only store failures count: a validation error or a duplicate tenant id is not a Redis problem and must
not open the circuit. Test it with a fake clock and a fake store (no sleeping in tests): 3 failures →
the 4th call does not reach the store; advance the clock 5 s → one trial; a concurrent second call
during the trial is short-circuited. The same breaker class (cooldown 30 s) wraps the LLM client of
the advisor.

<!-- track:java -->
`resilience/CircuitBreaker.java` is generic (`call(Call<T>)` with an `isFailure` predicate and an
`onShortCircuit` callback); `store/GuardedStore.java` implements `Store`, and `AppConfig` exposes it as the
`@Primary` store bean, so every service gets the guarded one. State changes are `synchronized`; the slow
Redis call happens **outside** the lock.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `app/breaker.py` has a `call(fn)` method, a `threading.Lock` around state changes
and `time.monotonic` as the default clock (wall-clock time can jump). `GuardedStore` in `app/store.py`
has the same methods as `RedisStore`; `guard()` in `app/main.py` wires it.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `src/breaker.ts` wraps any async call. Node is single-threaded, but `await` still
interleaves requests, so the trial flag matters exactly as it does in Java and Python. `GuardedStore`
in `src/store.ts` implements `Store`; `guard()` in `src/wiring.ts` wires it.
<!-- /track -->

steps.title: Maintenance change: per-tenant fail modes (v1.1.0)
steps.content_md:
The breaker makes failures fast, but a fast `503` is still an outage. After the game day, tenants
disagreed about what they want during one (see ADR-0006). v1.1 lets each policy decide:
1. `policy.failMode`: `CLOSED` (the v1.0 behaviour: `503 limiter-unavailable`), `OPEN` (admit, marked
   degraded) or `LOCAL` (an in-memory limiter per instance, using **the same pure functions** from
   M2, marked degraded). Optional in requests; validation message
   `policy.failMode must be CLOSED, OPEN or LOCAL`.
2. **Backward compatible both ways:** the field is stored in the tenant hash; a hash written by v1.0
   has no `failMode` and reads as `CLOSED`. v1.0 ignores the extra field. A rolling deploy can mix versions.
3. **Last known good tenants:** `authenticate` caches each tenant it has seen, and uses the cache only
   when Redis is unavailable, so `OPEN`/`LOCAL` tenants can still be recognised. A key never seen
   before is refused.
4. **Degraded decisions** carry `X-RateLimit-Degraded: true` and `"degraded": true`; the counter
   `rateguard_degraded_decisions_total` counts them.
5. `/health` answers **`200`** with `status: DEGRADED` while Redis is down: restarting app instances
   cannot fix Redis, and a load balancer that removes every instance turns a degraded service into none.
6. `spec/openapi.yaml` → `version: 1.1.0` (`failMode`, `degraded`, `DEGRADED`, `/metrics`, `X-Request-ID`);
   `spec/adr/0006-…`; `CHANGELOG.md` → `## [1.1.0]`; bump the track's version.
7. Tests first: the breaker tests, resilience tests per fail mode (with a store that fails on demand and
   the breaker's fake clock), an integration test that a v1.0 hash reads as `CLOSED`, and one that a dead
   Redis costs three timeouts and then answers fast.
8. Re-run the game day on your branch, then release:
   `git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "RateGuard v1.1.0" && git push origin main --follow-tags`.

In the reference run (all three tracks gave the same pattern): v1.0 answered **every** check during the
freeze with `503` after ~1 s and `/health` with `503`; v1.1 answered `OPEN` tenants with `200` in 1–4 ms,
`LOCAL` tenants with 5 × `200` + 5 × `429`, `CLOSED` tenants with `503` after only three slow calls,
and `/health` with `200 DEGRADED` in a few milliseconds while 40 requests were in flight.

quiz.q: Why not simply echo any incoming `X-Request-ID`?
options: It would be too long for the log
Unvalidated input could inject newlines or fake fields into logs and headers
Request IDs must always be UUIDs
Browsers do not send it
quiz.explanation: Treat headers as user input. A strict allow-list regex keeps the useful case (a caller propagating its ID) and rejects the dangerous one.

quiz.q: Why is a frozen Redis worse than a stopped one?
options: A frozen Redis loses data
A stopped Redis refuses connections in a millisecond; a frozen one accepts them and never answers, so every call waits for the full timeout
A stopped Redis is restarted automatically
There is no difference with a timeout
quiz.explanation: Fast failures are cheap; slow failures pile up requests, threads and connections. That is why the game day uses `docker pause`, not `docker stop`.

quiz.q: In v1.0, `/health` returned `503` during the freeze. Why is that dangerous behind a load balancer?
options: The load balancer caches the 503
Every instance reports unhealthy at once, so the load balancer removes all of them and a Redis problem becomes a total outage, although restarting instances cannot fix Redis
`503` is not a valid health status
The health check takes too little time
quiz.explanation: Health checks should report what restarting or removing *this* instance would fix. v1.1 answers `200 DEGRADED` and exposes the dependency state for monitoring instead.

quiz.q: What does the circuit breaker change for a `CLOSED` tenant during the freeze?
options: Its requests are now allowed
Nothing at all
It still gets `503`, but after three slow calls the rest fail immediately instead of each waiting a second
It gets `429` instead of `503`
quiz.explanation: The breaker does not change the decision, only its cost. The decision is the tenant's `failMode`.

quiz.q: Why does a tenant hash written by v1.0 read as `failMode: CLOSED` in v1.1?
options: v1.1 rewrites all hashes at start-up
A missing field means the v1.0 behaviour, so old data keeps its meaning and no migration is needed
Redis adds default fields automatically
`CLOSED` is the safest mode for new tenants only
quiz.explanation: Additive, optional fields with a default equal to the old behaviour are the cheapest way to stay compatible during a rolling deploy and a rollback.

quiz.q: A `LOCAL` tenant has a limit of 5 per minute and 3 app instances. During a Redis outage, how many requests per minute can it get?
options: Up to 15: each instance enforces 5 on its own
Unlimited
quiz.explanation: A local fallback keeps *some* protection, not the exact limit. That trade-off is written down in ADR-0006 and in the API description.

recap: Request IDs, structured JSON logs and Prometheus counters as the minimum observability kit.
Running a game day with a realistic fault, measuring before and after, and writing a blameless post-mortem.
The circuit breaker pattern (closed, open, half-open) with deterministic tests.
Fail open vs fail closed vs local fallback as a per-tenant business decision.
Health checks that do not amplify a dependency failure.
Backward-compatible data changes in a key-value store and a semver minor release.

interview questions: you can now answer it with a system you built, measured and broke on purpose. The
retrospective is for you: it turns nine phases of experience into lessons you can explain in an interview.
