### Q5. Why must `TEST_REDIS_URL` never point at a Redis you do not own?
- [ ] The tests would be slower
- [x] The tests run `FLUSHDB` on database 15 before every test, deleting whatever someone else stored there
- [ ] Redis allows only one client
- [ ] The tests change the Redis configuration
> **Answer:** Destructive test setup is fine on an isolated database and an incident anywhere else. Check the port before you run the suite on a machine with other projects.

### Q6. Why break the code on purpose and watch a test fail?
- [ ] To practise git
- [x] A test that cannot fail gives false confidence; seeing it go red proves it checks the behaviour
- [ ] The coverage tool requires it
- [ ] To make CI slower
> **Answer:** It is a cheap form of mutation testing. Assistants often write tests that pass against any implementation.

## 7. What you learned
- The test pyramid and what each layer can and cannot prove.
- Parity tests: two implementations of the same maths kept in step by one shared timeline.
- Real-Redis integration tests with an isolated database and clean state per test.
- Testing atomicity where it matters: parallel requests from several instances against one Redis.
- Load testing for a property (the limit holds) and a number (p95 latency).
- Seeing a test fail on purpose, and coverage gates as a floor, not a goal.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-5 phase-4-end
git diff phase-3-end phase-4-end --stat    # the pending-list change + scripts/load-test.py: the tests were there all along
```

steps.title: Phase 5 · Continuous integration with GitHub Actions
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
"It passed on my machine" is not evidence. CI runs the same checks on a clean machine for every push
and pull request, so a broken change never reaches `main`. It is also the cheapest code reviewer you
will ever have. In this phase you grow the starter workflow into a real pipeline: path filters, a
reusable workflow, service containers for integration tests, caching, a coverage artefact and one
required status check.

Every keyword used here is explained slowly in **[docs/github-actions-explained.md](github-actions-explained.md)**.
Read it side by side with the YAML.

## 2. Objectives
- Explain triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, matrices, caching and artefacts.
- Write a **reusable workflow** (`workflow_call`) that runs one track's full check, and call it three times.
- Run integration tests in CI with a Redis **service container**.
- Skip unaffected tracks with a **path filter**, and still have a single required check (`ci-ok`).
- Validate the OpenAPI contract in CI and enable **Dependabot**.
- Protect `main` so a PR cannot be merged while CI is red.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 5.1 · Read the starter workflow
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It is a **matrix** over `[java, python, typescript]`; each matrix job
sets up one toolchain (`if: matrix.track == 'java'`), then runs `make install`, `make lint` and `make test`.
The same Makefile targets exist in every track, so CI does not need three different scripts.

### Step 5.2 · Create the reusable workflow
Create `.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml` with `on: workflow_call` and an input `track`. Give its job:
- `services:` `redis:7.4-alpine` with a health check (`redis-cli ping`) and a published port,
- `env:` `TEST_REDIS_URL: redis://localhost:6379/15` (the tests flush database 15 before each test),
- the setup steps from the starter, then `make install lint test`,
- `make coverage` (unit + integration + the 85 % gate),
- `actions/upload-artifact@v4` for the coverage report (`if: always()`).

### Step 5.3 · Rewrite `ci.yml` as an orchestrator
1. A `changes` job with `dorny/paths-filter@v3` that outputs `docs`, `shared`, `java`, `python`, `typescript`.
2. A `contract` job (only when shared files or docs change): `pipx run openapi-spec-validator spec/openapi.yaml`,
   `shellcheck` on `scripts/*.sh` and `python3 scripts/build-cms.py --check` (the course export must match `docs/`).
3. Three jobs `java`, `python`, `typescript`, each `uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml`
   with `if:` on its path output.
4. A final `ci-ok` job with `if: always()` and `needs:` on all of them that fails when any result is
   `failure` or `cancelled`. Skipped is fine.

The reference is at `git show phase-5-end:.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

### Step 5.4 · Lint your workflows before pushing
```bash
# https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint  (Go binary; also available via Homebrew / Docker)
go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest
actionlint                       # run from the repo root
```
`actionlint` catches typos in expressions, unknown inputs, bad `needs` and shell bugs (via shellcheck)
before GitHub ever sees them.

### Step 5.5 · Dependabot
Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with one entry per ecosystem: `maven` in `/tracks/java`, `pip` in
`/tracks/python`, `npm` in `/tracks/typescript`, and `github-actions` in `/`. Group minor + patch updates
so you get one PR per ecosystem per week.

### Step 5.6 · Protect `main`
In your fork: **Settings → Branches → Add branch ruleset** (or classic rule) for `main`:
- Require a pull request before merging.
- Require status checks to pass → add **`ci-ok`** (it appears after the first run).
- Block force pushes.

Because skipped jobs count as success, a docs-only PR still gets a green `ci-ok` quickly.

### Step 5.7 · Prove it works
Open a PR that breaks one test in **one** track: only that track's job runs (path filter) and `ci-ok`
goes red, so the merge button is blocked. Fix it and watch it go green. Then open a PR that only touches
`spec/openapi.yaml`: all jobs run, because a contract change affects every track.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Explain a workflow line by line
```text
Explain this GitHub Actions workflow line by line for a beginner. For every expression ${{ ... }} say
when it is evaluated and what value it will have on a pull_request event from a fork:
<paste .github/workflows/ci.yml>
```
**Verify the output by:** comparing each claim with the official docs (docs.github.com/actions, the
"Workflow syntax" and "Contexts" pages) and with `docs/github-actions-explained.md`. Assistants often
mix up `github.ref` on pull requests and the secrets available to forks.

### Prompt 2: Debug a red job
```text
My GitHub Actions job fails. Here is the failing step's log (last 80 lines) and the workflow file.
Tell me the most likely cause, how to reproduce it locally with the same commands, and the smallest fix.
<paste log> <paste YAML>
```
**Verify the output by:** reproducing the failure locally with the same `make` target first. If you
cannot reproduce it, re-run the job with debug logging (**Re-run jobs → Enable debug logging**) before
changing anything.

### Prompt 3: Review for security
```text
Review this workflow for security problems: overly broad permissions, secrets exposed to pull requests
from forks, unpinned third-party actions, script injection through ${{ github.event.* }} in run steps.
<paste YAML>
```
**Verify the output by:** checking the `permissions:` block (we use `contents: read` by default), and
searching the YAML for `${{ github.event` inside `run:`. Untrusted strings must go through `env:` first.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `reusable-track-ci.yml` + rewritten `ci.yml`; `actionlint` passes locally.
- [ ] A green run where all three tracks ran integration tests with service containers.
- [ ] A PR touching one track that skips the others (screenshot of the run graph).
- [ ] Branch protection on `main` requiring `ci-ok`.
- [ ] `.github/dependabot.yml`.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. What does `on: workflow_call` mean?
- [ ] The workflow runs when someone calls the repository's API
- [x] The workflow can be used as a reusable workflow by other workflows (`jobs.<id>.uses`)
- [ ] The workflow runs on every push
- [ ] The workflow can only be run manually
> **Answer:** A reusable workflow is like a function: it declares `inputs`, and the caller passes them with `with:`.

### Q2. Why is `ci-ok` the only required check instead of every job?
- [ ] GitHub allows only one required check
- [x] With path filters some jobs are skipped; one aggregator job gives a stable name that is green when nothing failed
- [ ] It makes CI faster
- [ ] Reusable workflows cannot be required checks
> **Answer:** Required checks are matched by name. An aggregator with `if: always()` survives jobs being skipped or renamed.

### Q3. How do integration tests reach Redis in CI?
- [ ] They use the in-memory store
- [ ] They connect to a free cloud Redis
- [x] A `services:` container runs next to the job and its port is published on `localhost`
- [ ] Docker Compose is started inside the test
> **Answer:** Service containers live for one job, are health-checked before steps start, and are thrown away afterwards.

### Q4. What does `cache: npm` (or `maven`/`pip`) in a setup action do?
- [ ] Caches the build output
- [x] Restores the package download cache keyed by a hash of the lock file, so installs are faster
- [ ] Commits `node_modules` to the repo
- [ ] Skips the install step
> **Answer:** The key changes when `package-lock.json` / `pom.xml` / `requirements-dev.txt` changes, so you never get stale dependencies.

### Q5. Which default `permissions` block is safest for a CI workflow that only reads code?
- [ ] `permissions: write-all`
- [x] `permissions: contents: read`
- [ ] No block at all
- [ ] `permissions: packages: write`
> **Answer:** Least privilege. Jobs that need more (e.g. pushing images) ask for it explicitly, as `deploy.yml` does in Phase 6.

## 7. What you learned
- Workflow anatomy: triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, `defaults`, `concurrency`.
- Reusable workflows with inputs, and an orchestrator workflow that calls them.
- Service containers for real integration tests in CI.
- Path filters plus an aggregator job for fast and safe required checks.
- Caching, artefacts, actionlint, Dependabot and branch protection.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-6 phase-5-end
git diff phase-4-end phase-5-end -- .github/
git checkout phase-5-end -- .github/          # take the reference workflows
```

steps.title: Phase 6 · Containerise, deliver and (optionally) deploy
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A container image is the unit you actually ship: the same bytes run on your laptop, in CI and in
the cloud. In this phase you write a production-grade Dockerfile, run the whole stack with one
command, prove it with a black-box smoke test, run **two instances of your track against one Redis**
the way it would run in production, and publish versioned images to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR)
automatically on every release tag. Deploying to the cloud is **optional**: everything graded in this
phase works offline on your laptop.

## 2. Objectives
- Write a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile with a `HEALTHCHECK` for your track that ships the shared Lua scripts.
- Add your app to `docker-compose.yml` as a profile and start the stack with `docker compose --profile <track> up`.
- Run the language-agnostic smoke test against your container (and against the other tracks' images).
- Run two instances behind one Redis (`pair` profile) and repeat the load test.
- Add a Docker build + smoke job to CI.
- Write `deploy.yml`: on a `v*.*.*` tag, build and push images to GHCR; optionally trigger a Render
  deploy that is **skipped gracefully** when no secret is configured.
- Cut release **v1.0.0** with a CHANGELOG entry.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 6.1 · The Dockerfile (build context = repository root)
All tracks copy the shared Lua scripts into the image, so the build context is the repo root and the
Dockerfile lives in the track: `docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile .`. Rules:
- **Multi-stage:** compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage.
- **Dependencies before source:** copy the manifest, install, then copy `src`, so code changes reuse the dependency layer.
- **Non-root user**, `EXPOSE 8080`, `HEALTHCHECK` hitting `/health`, `COPY spec/lua ./lua` and `LUA_DIR=/app/lua`.

<!-- track:java -->
```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/java/pom.xml tracks/java/checkstyle.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY tracks/java/src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests -Dcheckstyle.skip -Djacoco.skip=true \
    && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination /extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
ENV PORT=8080 LUA_DIR=/app/lua JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError"
WORKDIR /app
RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 app && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid app --no-create-home app
COPY --from=build /extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/application/ ./
COPY spec/lua ./lua
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health > /dev/null || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```
(abridged; the full file installs `curl` and sets the health-check timings)
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/python/requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PORT=8080 LUA_DIR=/app/lua
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels \
    && useradd --system --uid 10001 --no-create-home appuser
COPY tracks/python/app ./app
COPY spec/lua ./lua
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK CMD python -c "import urllib.request,sys; sys.exit(0 if urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health', timeout=2).status == 200 else 1)"
CMD ["python", "-m", "app"]
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
COPY tracks/typescript/tsconfig.json tracks/typescript/tsconfig.build.json ./
COPY tracks/typescript/src ./src
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=8080 LUA_DIR=/app/lua
WORKDIR /app
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund && npm cache clean --force
COPY --from=build /build/dist ./dist
COPY spec/lua ./lua
USER node
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
```
<!-- /track -->

The repository's `.dockerignore` keeps the build context small and excludes `.env`, so local secrets
never reach the Docker daemon. Build and check the size and user:
```bash
docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile -t rateguard-<track>:local .
docker image ls rateguard-<track>
docker run --rm --entrypoint id rateguard-<track>:local      # must NOT be uid=0
```

### Step 6.2 · Compose profiles: one command for the whole stack
Add a service per track to `docker-compose.yml` under a **profile**, sharing one block of environment
variables (a YAML anchor `x-app-env`), `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, and port
`${APP_PORT:-8080}:8080`. Inside Compose the app reaches Redis as `redis://redis:6379/0`, not
`localhost`. The Compose file sets a **local-only** `ADMIN_TOKEN` through `${VAR:-default}`, so
`docker compose up` works out of the box. A real deployment sets its own value: the default is
public, in this repository. Redis runs with `--appendonly yes`, so tenants and keys survive a restart.
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

### Step 6.3 · Smoke test (the same for every track)
```bash
scripts/smoke-test.sh                      # default http://localhost:8080
```
It checks 53 behaviours with only `bash`, `curl` and `xargs`: health, `404` and `401` as
`problem+json`, creating a token-bucket tenant (the key is shown once and never again), a duplicate
id (`409`), an id that could break a Redis key (`400`), a check with all `X-RateLimit-*` headers, a
cost above the limit (`422`), an unknown key (`401`), three allowed `hello`s and a `429` with
`Retry-After`, a sliding-window tenant whose denied check is still a `200` answer, **parallel**
checks against a limit of 5 (exactly 5 allowed), reset, key rotation (the old key dies at once), a
policy change, usage, advice, and deleting a tenant (its key is revoked). It creates its own uniquely
named tenants and deletes them at the end, so it is safe to run repeatedly. Against a deployment,
pass the admin token as `SMOKE_ADMIN_TOKEN`.

Because the contract and the scripts are shared, try another track's image against the same Redis:
`docker compose stop app-<yours>` and `docker compose --profile python up -d`. Same results. Also run
the AI fallback check:
```bash
AI_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 LLM_TIMEOUT_MS=1000 docker compose --profile <track> up -d --wait
EXPECT_FALLBACK=true scripts/smoke-test.sh      # the advice reports provider "rules" and fallback: true
```

### Step 6.4 · Two instances, one Redis
The `pair` profile starts two containers of the same image on ports 8081 and 8082:
```bash
TRACK=<track> docker compose --profile pair up -d --build --wait
python3 scripts/load-test.py                   # http://localhost:8081 and http://localhost:8082
```
`allowed` must equal the limit, exactly as in Phase 4, now with real containers and a real network.
Stop one of the two in the middle of a run (`docker compose stop app-b`): the other keeps enforcing
the same limit, because no instance holds any state.

### Step 6.5 · CI: build the image and smoke-test it
Add a `docker` job (matrix over tracks) to `ci.yml`: `docker/setup-buildx-action`,
`docker/build-push-action` with `load: true` and the GitHub Actions layer cache (`cache-from/to: type=gha`),
then `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --no-build --wait`, the smoke test, logs on failure and `down -v`.

### Step 6.6 · Continuous delivery to GHCR: `deploy.yml`
Trigger on `push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]`. The job needs `permissions: packages: write` and logs in to
`ghcr.io` with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`; no personal token required. Image names must be lower-case
(the org is `AICanCode-org`), so compute `ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/rateguard-<track>`.
`docker/metadata-action` turns tag `v1.0.0` into image tags `1.0.0`, `1.0`, `sha-<short>` and `latest`.
Read `docs/github-actions-explained.md` §9–§12 for every detail.

### Step 6.7 · Release v1.0.0
```bash
# update CHANGELOG.md: move "Unreleased" items under "## [1.0.0] - <date>"
git commit -am "chore(release): v1.0.0"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "RateGuard v1.0.0"
git push origin main --follow-tags
```
Watch **Actions → Deploy**: three images appear under your profile's **Packages**. New GHCR packages
are **private** by default. Make one public (Package settings → Change visibility) if a host should pull
it without credentials.

### Step 6.8 · OPTIONAL: deploy to a free tier
You do not need a cloud account to finish this course. If you want a public URL:

| Piece | Free option | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App | **Render** web service from an *existing image* (`ghcr.io/<you>/rateguard-<track>:latest`) | Free instances spin down after 15 minutes without traffic; the next request takes about a minute (cold start). |
| Redis | **Upstash** Redis free tier, or Render Key Value (free) | Use the TLS URL (`rediss://…`) as `REDIS_URL`. Free plans limit commands per day and memory, and some do not persist data: read the limits, and remember tenants live in Redis. |
| Secrets | Render env vars | Set your own `ADMIN_TOKEN` (`openssl rand -hex 32`). Never reuse the Compose default. |
| LLM | none (rules), or a free Gemini / Groq key | `AI_PROVIDER=llm`, `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` as Render env vars. Only usage numbers are sent, but say so in your README. |

Free-tier limits change. Check each provider's pricing page before you rely on it. Fly.io is **not**
used: at the time of writing it needs a payment method and bills usage, with no free tier for new accounts.

To let CI deploy for you:
1. Render → your service → **Settings → Deploy Hook**: copy the URL.
2. GitHub → **Settings → Environments → New environment `production`** (optionally add yourself as a
   required reviewer). Add the **secret** `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` and the **variables** `RENDER_APP_URL`
   (e.g. `https://rateguard-xyz.onrender.com`) and `DEPLOY_TRACK` (`java`, `python` or `typescript`).
   Optionally add the secret `SMOKE_ADMIN_TOKEN` (your live `ADMIN_TOKEN`) so the full smoke test runs
   against the live app; without it only `/health` is checked.
3. Push a tag. The `render` job calls the hook with `imgURL=` set to the exact version, waits for
   `/health`, and runs the smoke test against the live URL. Without the secret the job prints a notice
   and **succeeds**, so forks without cloud accounts stay green.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Review my Dockerfile
```text
Review this Dockerfile for a <Spring Boot 4 / FastAPI / Fastify> service that loads Redis Lua scripts
from LUA_DIR. Check: multi-stage, layer caching order, non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, image size, secrets
leaking into layers, pinned base image versions, and anything that would differ between my laptop
(amd64/arm64) and CI. <paste Dockerfile>
```
**Verify the output by:** rebuilding and measuring: `docker image ls` (size), `docker run --rm --entrypoint id`
(uid), `docker history` (no secrets, small layers), `docker run --rm --entrypoint ls rateguard-<track>:local /app/lua`
(both scripts present) and `docker compose up --wait` (health check passes).

### Prompt 2: Explain the deploy workflow's security model
```text
In this workflow <paste deploy.yml>, which token pushes to GHCR, what can it do, and for how long?
Are RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL and SMOKE_ADMIN_TOKEN exposed to pull requests from forks? What would
happen if someone pushed a tag from a fork?
```
**Verify the output by:** reading the GitHub docs pages "Automatic token authentication" and "Using secrets
in GitHub Actions" (secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks), and checking that
`packages: write` appears only on the image job.

### Prompt 3: Cold start and a free Redis
```text
My container works locally but on Render /health times out for the first minute after idle, then works,
and after a few days all my tenants are gone. Explain cold starts on free tiers, what my smoke test
should do about them, how to tell a cold start apart from a crash in the logs, and what a free Redis
plan may do with my data (eviction, persistence, command limits).
```
**Verify the output by:** reading your service's Render logs for the boot sequence (scripts loaded,
listening on port), timing `curl -w '%{time_total}' $URL/health` after 20 minutes idle, and checking
your Redis provider's documentation for persistence and eviction on the free plan.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `tracks/<track>/Dockerfile` (multi-stage, non-root, HEALTHCHECK, Lua scripts in `/app/lua`).
- [ ] `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait` + `scripts/smoke-test.sh`: all checks pass,
  and `EXPECT_FALLBACK=true` passes with an unreachable LLM.
- [ ] The load test against the `pair` profile: `allowed` = the limit.
- [ ] CI `docker` job green; `deploy.yml` pushed images to GHCR for tag `v1.0.0`.
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` with `[1.0.0]`; `docs/runbook.md` with start/stop/rollback/rotate-token steps.
- [ ] Optional: a live URL in your README and a green `render` job.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why do the Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest before the source code?
- [ ] Docker requires that order
- [x] So that the dependency layer is cached and only rebuilt when the manifest changes
- [ ] To make the image smaller
- [ ] To run tests faster
> **Answer:** Layers are cached top-down; anything after a changed layer is rebuilt. Source changes often, dependencies rarely.

### Q2. Inside Docker Compose, which `REDIS_URL` does the app use?
- [ ] `redis://localhost:6379/0`
- [x] `redis://redis:6379/0` (the service name)
- [ ] `redis://127.0.0.1:6379/0`
- [ ] `redis://host.docker.internal:6379/0`
> **Answer:** Each container has its own `localhost`. Compose gives services DNS names on a shared network.

### Q3. Why does the build context have to be the repository root?
- [ ] Docker cannot build from sub-folders
- [x] The image needs `spec/lua/` as well as the track's code, and a build can only copy files inside its context
- [ ] To include the `.env` file
- [ ] To speed up the build
> **Answer:** The scripts are shared by all tracks, so they live outside `tracks/<track>`. `.dockerignore` keeps everything else (and `.env`) out of the context.

### Q4. A fork has no `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` secret. What does the `render` job do on a tag push?
- [ ] Fails the workflow
- [ ] Deploys to a default account
- [x] Prints a notice and succeeds; the image is still pushed to the fork's GHCR
- [ ] Waits for someone to add the secret
> **Answer:** Optional infrastructure must not make the pipeline red. Secrets are read into `env:` and tested with `if: env.X == ''`.

### Q5. You stop one of the two `pair` instances during a load test. What happens to the limit?
- [ ] It doubles, because the other instance forgets the shared state
- [ ] It halves
- [x] Nothing: all state is in Redis, so the remaining instance enforces exactly the same limit
- [ ] Requests fail until both are back
> **Answer:** Stateless app instances can come and go (deploys, crashes, autoscaling) without changing any decision.

### Q6. Why must a deployment never use the `ADMIN_TOKEN` from `docker-compose.yml`?
- [ ] It is too short
- [x] It is public in the repository, so anyone could create tenants, read usage and reset limits on your service
- [ ] Render rejects it
- [ ] It expires after 30 days
> **Answer:** Defaults are for laptops; deployments get their own token from the host's environment variables.

## 7. What you learned
- Production Dockerfiles: multi-stage, layer caching, non-root, health checks, `.dockerignore`, shared files in the image.
- Compose profiles to run any track, or two instances of one, against the same Redis with one command.
- Black-box smoke tests that work for any implementation of a contract.
- Image builds with layer caching in CI, and delivery to GHCR with the built-in token on version tags.
- Optional, secret-gated deployment that degrades gracefully, plus free-tier trade-offs (cold starts, Redis limits).
- Semantic versioning and a CHANGELOG-driven release.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-7 phase-6-end          # == v1.0.0
git checkout phase-6-end -- tracks/<track>/Dockerfile docker-compose.yml scripts/smoke-test.sh
git checkout phase-6-end -- .github/workflows/deploy.yml
```

steps.title: Phase 7 · Observability, game day and resilience (v1.1.0)
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Shipping v1.0.0 is the start, not the end. In production you have to answer "is it working right now,
and if not, why?" without attaching a debugger. That needs three things: **logs** you can search,
**metrics** you can graph, and a **request ID** that ties a tenant's complaint ("we got 503s at 19:42")
to log lines. RateGuard sits in front of other people's traffic and depends on one thing it does not
control, Redis, so you will run a **game day** where Redis freezes, measure what tenants feel, and
discover that "fail closed" (ADR-0004) hurts more than the ADR predicted. You fix it with a **circuit
breaker** and your first **maintenance change**, driven by what tenants told you: a per-tenant
`failMode`, released backward compatibly as v1.1.0.

## 2. Objectives
- Give every request an `X-Request-ID` (reuse a safe incoming one, or generate a UUID) and put it in every log line.
- Emit structured **JSON logs**: one object per line, one access-log line per request.
- Expose `/metrics` in Prometheus text format with eight counters that are identical in every track.
- Run a **game day**: freeze Redis with `docker pause`, measure checks and `/health`, write a short blameless post-mortem.
- Add a Redis **circuit breaker** (3 failures in a row → open for `REDIS_BREAKER_COOLDOWN_MS` → one half-open trial) and reuse it for the LLM.
- Ship a backward-compatible change: `policy.failMode` (`CLOSED` | `OPEN` | `LOCAL`), degraded decisions,
  `/health` `DEGRADED`, OpenAPI 1.1.0, ADR-0006, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
- Review and merge one Dependabot PR.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 7.1 · Request IDs
Rule (shared by all tracks): if the incoming `X-Request-ID` matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, echo it;
otherwise generate a UUID. Never echo arbitrary input: a header containing a newline could inject
fake log lines or headers.

<!-- track:java -->
A `OncePerRequestFilter` (`web/RequestIdFilter.java`) sets the response header, puts `requestId` in
the SLF4J **MDC** (so every log line in that request carries it) and logs one `rateguard.access` line
with `method`, `path`, `status` and `durationMs` using the fluent API
`LOG.atInfo().addKeyValue("status", …).log()`. `@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` makes it the first
filter, so even a `401` or a `404` gets an ID.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A Starlette middleware (`app/observability.py`) stores the ID in `request.state`, sets the response
header and logs one `rateguard.access` record with `extra={"fields": {...}}`. The middleware wraps the
whole app, so error responses (`400`, `401`, `404`, `503`) carry the header too.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Fastify has request IDs built in: `genReqId` (calling `incomingOrNewId()` from `src/observability.ts`)
with `requestIdHeader: false`, so we validate the incoming value ourselves, and a `LogController` with `requestIdLogLabel: "requestId"`.
An `onSend` hook copies `request.id` into the `X-Request-ID` response header.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 7.2 · JSON logs
<!-- track:java -->
One property: `logging.structured.format.console=logstash` in `application.properties`. MDC values
and key/value pairs become JSON fields.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A small `logging.Formatter` subclass (`JsonFormatter`) that `json.dumps` `ts`, `level`, `logger`, `msg`
and the `fields`; installed by `configure_logging()` at startup.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Nothing to add: Fastify's logger (pino) already writes JSON, one line per event (`incoming request`,
`request completed` with `responseTime`).
<!-- /track -->

**Never log secrets.** API keys, the admin token, the `Authorization` and `X-API-Key` headers and the
LLM API key must not appear in any log line. Grep for them after the smoke test
(`docker compose logs app-<track> | grep -E 'rg_[0-9a-f]{32}|Bearer'` must print nothing).

Check it:
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
curl -s -H 'X-Request-ID: demo-123' localhost:8080/health -o /dev/null -D - | grep -i x-request-id
docker compose logs app-<track> | grep demo-123
```

### Step 7.3 · `/metrics`
Eight counters, same names in all tracks (see `GET /metrics` in `spec/openapi.yaml`):

| Counter | Incremented when |
|---|---|
| `rateguard_decisions_allowed_total` | a check was allowed |
| `rateguard_decisions_denied_total` | a check was denied (a spike here is a tenant hitting its limit) |
| `rateguard_degraded_decisions_total` | a check was decided by the tenant's `failMode` because Redis was unavailable (Step 7.6) |
| `rateguard_store_errors_total` | a Redis call failed (refused, timed out, broken connection) |
| `rateguard_store_short_circuits_total` | the circuit breaker skipped a Redis call (Step 7.5) |
| `rateguard_tenants_created_total` | `POST /admin/tenants` created a tenant |
| `rateguard_ai_fallback_total` | an advice request fell back to the offline rules |
| `rateguard_llm_short_circuits_total` | the circuit breaker skipped an LLM call |

They are hand-rolled on purpose: the Prometheus text format is just
```text
# HELP rateguard_store_errors_total Redis calls that failed (refused, timed out, broken connection).
# TYPE rateguard_store_errors_total counter
rateguard_store_errors_total 3
```
In a bigger service you would use Micrometer (Java), `prometheus-client` (Python) or `prom-client` (Node).
`/metrics` is public in this course project; in production you would restrict it to the scraper's network.

### Step 7.4 · Game day: Redis freezes
A dead Redis is easy: the connection is refused and the error comes back in a millisecond. A
**frozen** Redis is worse: the kernel still accepts connections, but nothing answers, so every command
waits for the full `REDIS_TIMEOUT_MS` (1 s). That is what a Redis stuck in a slow command, a full disk,
a long fork for a snapshot or a network partition looks like. `docker pause` produces exactly that.
1. Start the stack at v1.0.0: `git switch --detach v1.0.0`, `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait`.
2. Get the script from the reference: `git show phase-7-end:scripts/game-day.sh > /tmp/game-day.sh && chmod +x /tmp/game-day.sh`,
   then `/tmp/game-day.sh <track>`. It creates three tenants with a limit of 5 per 60 s and the fail
   modes `CLOSED`, `OPEN` and `LOCAL` (v1.0 ignores the field: every tenant is effectively `CLOSED`),
   then runs phases of 10 requests per tenant: **baseline**, Redis **frozen**, `/health` while 40
   requests are in flight, Redis **back** immediately, and Redis back **after 6 s**.
3. Write down for each phase: status codes, average and maximum latency, how many decisions were
   degraded, `/health`'s status and latency, the warnings in the logs, and (from v1.1) the counters.
   What did tenants get? What did the load balancer get from `/health`, and what would it do with it?
4. Write `docs/postmortem-<date>-redis-freeze.md`: summary, impact, timeline, root cause, what went
   well, what to improve, action items. Blameless: describe systems, not people. Read the reference
   post-mortem **after** writing yours (`git show phase-7-end:docs/postmortem-2026-10-02-redis-freeze.md`).

### Step 7.5 · Fix: a circuit breaker in front of Redis
Wrap the store in a `GuardedStore` that sends every call through a `CircuitBreaker`:
- **CLOSED:** calls go through. 3 store failures **in a row** open the circuit.
- **OPEN:** calls fail immediately with "store unavailable" for `REDIS_BREAKER_COOLDOWN_MS` (5 s), and
  `rateguard_store_short_circuits_total` is incremented. No request waits for a timeout any more.
- **HALF-OPEN:** after the cooldown, exactly **one** trial call goes through. Success closes the circuit;
  failure re-opens it for another cooldown.

Only store failures count: a validation error or a duplicate tenant id is not a Redis problem and must
not open the circuit. Test it with a fake clock and a fake store (no sleeping in tests): 3 failures →
the 4th call does not reach the store; advance the clock 5 s → one trial; a concurrent second call
during the trial is short-circuited. The same breaker class (cooldown 30 s) wraps the LLM client of
the advisor.

<!-- track:java -->
`resilience/CircuitBreaker.java` is generic (`call(Call<T>)` with an `isFailure` predicate and an
`onShortCircuit` callback); `store/GuardedStore.java` implements `Store`, and `AppConfig` exposes it as the
`@Primary` store bean, so every service gets the guarded one. State changes are `synchronized`; the slow
Redis call happens **outside** the lock.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `app/breaker.py` has a `call(fn)` method, a `threading.Lock` around state changes
and `time.monotonic` as the default clock (wall-clock time can jump). `GuardedStore` in `app/store.py`
has the same methods as `RedisStore`; `guard()` in `app/main.py` wires it.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
`CircuitBreaker` in `src/breaker.ts` wraps any async call. Node is single-threaded, but `await` still
interleaves requests, so the trial flag matters exactly as it does in Java and Python. `GuardedStore`
in `src/store.ts` implements `Store`; `guard()` in `src/wiring.ts` wires it.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 7.6 · Maintenance change: per-tenant fail modes (v1.1.0)
The breaker makes failures fast, but a fast `503` is still an outage. After the game day, tenants
disagreed about what they want during one (see ADR-0006). v1.1 lets each policy decide:
1. `policy.failMode`: `CLOSED` (the v1.0 behaviour: `503 limiter-unavailable`), `OPEN` (admit, marked
   degraded) or `LOCAL` (an in-memory limiter per instance, using **the same pure functions** from
   M2, marked degraded). Optional in requests; validation message
   `policy.failMode must be CLOSED, OPEN or LOCAL`.
2. **Backward compatible both ways:** the field is stored in the tenant hash; a hash written by v1.0
   has no `failMode` and reads as `CLOSED`. v1.0 ignores the extra field. A rolling deploy can mix versions.
3. **Last known good tenants:** `authenticate` caches each tenant it has seen, and uses the cache only
   when Redis is unavailable, so `OPEN`/`LOCAL` tenants can still be recognised. A key never seen
   before is refused.
4. **Degraded decisions** carry `X-RateLimit-Degraded: true` and `"degraded": true`; the counter
   `rateguard_degraded_decisions_total` counts them.
5. `/health` answers **`200`** with `status: DEGRADED` while Redis is down: restarting app instances
   cannot fix Redis, and a load balancer that removes every instance turns a degraded service into none.
6. `spec/openapi.yaml` → `version: 1.1.0` (`failMode`, `degraded`, `DEGRADED`, `/metrics`, `X-Request-ID`);
   `spec/adr/0006-…`; `CHANGELOG.md` → `## [1.1.0]`; bump the track's version.
7. Tests first: the breaker tests, resilience tests per fail mode (with a store that fails on demand and
   the breaker's fake clock), an integration test that a v1.0 hash reads as `CLOSED`, and one that a dead
   Redis costs three timeouts and then answers fast.
8. Re-run the game day on your branch, then release:
   `git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "RateGuard v1.1.0" && git push origin main --follow-tags`.

In the reference run (all three tracks gave the same pattern): v1.0 answered **every** check during the
freeze with `503` after ~1 s and `/health` with `503`; v1.1 answered `OPEN` tenants with `200` in 1–4 ms,
`LOCAL` tenants with 5 × `200` + 5 × `429`, `CLOSED` tenants with `503` after only three slow calls,
and `/health` with `200 DEGRADED` in a few milliseconds while 40 requests were in flight.

### Step 7.7 · Merge a Dependabot PR
Pick one grouped update. Read its release notes, check that CI is green **including integration tests**,
run it locally if it is a major version, then merge. Write down in `AI_LOG.md` or the PR what you checked.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Structured logging setup
```text
I run a <Spring Boot 4 | FastAPI | Fastify 5> service. Show me the smallest change that makes every log
line a single JSON object with ts, level, logger, msg and a requestId taken from a validated
X-Request-ID header (regex ^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$, else a new UUID), plus one access-log line per
request with method, path, status and durationMs. No new dependencies unless unavoidable.
```
**Verify the output by:** running the smoke test and piping the logs through `jq -c .` (every line must
parse), sending `X-Request-ID: $(printf 'a\nb')` and checking a UUID comes back instead, and grepping the
logs for `rg_` and `Bearer` (no matches).

### Prompt 2: Review my circuit breaker
```text
Here is my circuit breaker for Redis calls: <paste>. Requirements: 3 consecutive store failures open
it; while open, calls fail immediately for REDIS_BREAKER_COOLDOWN_MS; then exactly one trial call; a
success closes it, a failure re-opens it; only store errors count as failures (not validation errors or
duplicates); the slow Redis call must not run while holding a lock. Find bugs, especially races between
concurrent requests in the half-open state, and give a failing test for each.
```
**Verify the output by:** turning each claimed race into a unit test with a fake clock and two
interleaved calls. Keep only findings whose test fails before your fix and passes after it. Reject
suggestions to add `sleep` to tests.

### Prompt 3: Is this change backward compatible?
```text
v1.0 of my service stores tenants as Redis hashes without a failMode field; v1.1 adds failMode (CLOSED,
OPEN, LOCAL; missing means CLOSED) and a degraded flag in responses. During a rolling deploy, v1.0 and
v1.1 instances share one Redis. List every way this can go wrong: a v1.1 instance reading a v1.0 hash, a
v1.0 instance reading or rewriting a v1.1 hash (does it drop the field?), clients that parse responses
strictly, and what a rollback to v1.0 does.
```
**Verify the output by:** testing the claims: create a tenant with v1.1 and `failMode: LOCAL`, change its
policy with the v1.0 image against the same Redis, then read it with v1.1 again (does `failMode` survive?);
create one with v1.0 and read it with v1.1 (`CLOSED`). Write down what you found in the PR; it decides
whether a rollback is safe.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `X-Request-ID` on every response (including errors) and in every log line; logs are JSON; no secrets in logs.
- [ ] `/metrics` with the eight counters.
- [ ] Game-day notes and `docs/postmortem-<date>-redis-freeze.md` with numbers for v1.0 and your fix.
- [ ] The Redis circuit breaker with unit tests (fake clock, no sleeps); the LLM uses the same breaker.
- [ ] Fail modes: `failMode` in the API, degraded decisions with the header and flag, `/health` `DEGRADED`, ADR-0006.
- [ ] OpenAPI 1.1.0, CHANGELOG `[1.1.0]`, tag `v1.1.0`, images published.
- [ ] One Dependabot PR reviewed and merged.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why not simply echo any incoming `X-Request-ID`?
- [ ] It would be too long for the log
- [x] Unvalidated input could inject newlines or fake fields into logs and headers
- [ ] Request IDs must always be UUIDs
- [ ] Browsers do not send it
> **Answer:** Treat headers as user input. A strict allow-list regex keeps the useful case (a caller propagating its ID) and rejects the dangerous one.

### Q2. Why is a frozen Redis worse than a stopped one?
- [ ] A frozen Redis loses data
- [x] A stopped Redis refuses connections in a millisecond; a frozen one accepts them and never answers, so every call waits for the full timeout
- [ ] A stopped Redis is restarted automatically
- [ ] There is no difference with a timeout
> **Answer:** Fast failures are cheap; slow failures pile up requests, threads and connections. That is why the game day uses `docker pause`, not `docker stop`.

### Q3. In v1.0, `/health` returned `503` during the freeze. Why is that dangerous behind a load balancer?
- [ ] The load balancer caches the 503
- [x] Every instance reports unhealthy at once, so the load balancer removes all of them and a Redis problem becomes a total outage, although restarting instances cannot fix Redis
- [ ] `503` is not a valid health status
- [ ] The health check takes too little time
> **Answer:** Health checks should report what restarting or removing *this* instance would fix. v1.1 answers `200 DEGRADED` and exposes the dependency state for monitoring instead.

### Q4. What does the circuit breaker change for a `CLOSED` tenant during the freeze?
- [ ] Its requests are now allowed
- [ ] Nothing at all
- [x] It still gets `503`, but after three slow calls the rest fail immediately instead of each waiting a second
- [ ] It gets `429` instead of `503`
> **Answer:** The breaker does not change the decision, only its cost. The decision is the tenant's `failMode`.

### Q5. Why does a tenant hash written by v1.0 read as `failMode: CLOSED` in v1.1?
- [ ] v1.1 rewrites all hashes at start-up
- [x] A missing field means the v1.0 behaviour, so old data keeps its meaning and no migration is needed
- [ ] Redis adds default fields automatically
- [ ] `CLOSED` is the safest mode for new tenants only
> **Answer:** Additive, optional fields with a default equal to the old behaviour are the cheapest way to stay compatible during a rolling deploy and a rollback.

### Q6. A `LOCAL` tenant has a limit of 5 per minute and 3 app instances. During a Redis outage, how many requests per minute can it get?
- [ ] 5
- [ ] 0
- [x] Up to 15: each instance enforces 5 on its own
- [ ] Unlimited
> **Answer:** A local fallback keeps *some* protection, not the exact limit. That trade-off is written down in ADR-0006 and in the API description.

## 7. What you learned
- Request IDs, structured JSON logs and Prometheus counters as the minimum observability kit.
- Running a game day with a realistic fault, measuring before and after, and writing a blameless post-mortem.
- The circuit breaker pattern (closed, open, half-open) with deterministic tests.
- Fail open vs fail closed vs local fallback as a per-tenant business decision.
- Health checks that do not amplify a dependency failure.
- Backward-compatible data changes in a key-value store and a semver minor release.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-8 phase-7-end          # == v1.1.0
git diff v1.0.0 v1.1.0 --stat                 # the whole maintenance change
git show phase-7-end:docs/postmortem-2026-10-02-redis-freeze.md
```

steps.title: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
A recruiter spends about a minute on your repository. "Another rate limiter tutorial" is forgettable;
a README that tells the story (the problem, the atomicity and failure design, the trade-offs, the
evidence, what you would do next) is proof that you can design, test, ship and operate software, and
that you use AI responsibly. "Design a rate limiter" is also one of the most common system-design
interview questions: you can now answer it with a system you built, measured and broke on purpose. The
retrospective is for you: it turns nine phases of experience into lessons you can explain in an interview.

## 2. Objectives
- Rewrite the README top section as a **case study** with real numbers from your project.
- Write a short **retrospective** (what went well, what didn't, what you'd change).
- Summarise your **AI_LOG** into three honest bullet points.
- Prepare a 2-minute walkthrough and answers to the distributed-systems questions interviewers ask about rate limiters.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 8.1 · Collect your evidence
```bash
git log --oneline | wc -l                       # commits
git tag -l 'v*'                                  # releases
make coverage                                    # coverage % per track
scripts/smoke-test.sh | tail -1                  # e.g. "Result: 60 passed, 0 failed"
python3 scripts/load-test.py | tail -3           # allowed = limit, p95 latency
curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep _total     # counters after a demo session
```
Also grab: a screenshot of the CI run graph, the GHCR package page, your game-day numbers for v1.0
and v1.1, and (optionally) your live URL.

### Step 8.2 · README case study
At the top of `README.md`, before the setup instructions, add a section with:
1. **One-line pitch** and a short `curl` session (create a tenant → 5 allowed, the 6th `429` with
   `Retry-After` → the headers → a degraded decision while Redis is paused).
2. **Problem → solution** in three sentences.
3. **Architecture** (link the Mermaid diagrams) and the **three decisions** you are proudest of, linking
   ADRs (for example atomic Lua scripts with pure-function twins, Redis `TIME` as the clock, hash tags,
   per-tenant fail modes).
4. **Correctness and security evidence:** which threats from Phase 1 are covered by which tests
   (over-admission across instances, clock drift, negative costs, key-pattern injection, stolen and
   rotated keys, timing attacks on the admin token).
5. **Quality evidence:** tests, coverage, CI badge, smoke test, load test.
6. **Operations:** health, metrics, request IDs, the game day and its post-mortem.
7. **How I used AI**, with honest examples of accepted and rejected suggestions.
8. **What I'd do next** (Redis Sentinel or Cluster, OpenTelemetry traces, per-key quotas per month,
   a client library that honours `Retry-After`, an admin UI…).

### Step 8.3 · Retrospective (`docs/retrospective.md`)
Use *Start / Stop / Continue* or *What went well / What didn't / What I'd change*. Include one
technical lesson (e.g. a timeout is a decision, not a safety net: a slow dependency costs more than a
dead one), one process lesson (test-first with a pending list, parity tests between two
implementations) and one AI lesson (an assistant confidently produced a non-atomic limiter or a
blocking `KEYS` call, and a test or the docs caught it).

### Step 8.4 · Practise the walkthrough
Record yourself (2 minutes): problem, architecture diagram, one interesting piece of code (the token
bucket Lua script or the circuit breaker are good ones), the test that proves it, the CI run, what you'd
do next. Then answer out loud:
- *Token bucket or sliding window, and why?* · *How do three instances share one limit?* · *Why Lua instead of `MULTI`?*
- *Whose clock do you trust?* · *What happens when Redis is slow, down or restarted?* · *How would you move to Redis Cluster?*
- *How do you store API keys?* · *How would you limit 10 million users instead of 200 tenants?* · *Where did AI help, and where did it mislead you?*

### Step 8.5 · Share it
Pin the repository on your GitHub profile, add the topics `rate-limiter`, `redis`, `lua`,
`<your-language>`, `docker`, `github-actions`, and post the case study (aicancode.org *Build in public*, LinkedIn).

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Draft the case study from evidence
```text
Write a README "case study" section (max 400 words) for my distributed rate limiter project from these
facts ONLY: <paste your evidence: test counts, coverage, load-test output, ADR titles, threats and the
tests that cover them, metrics, game-day numbers for v1.0 and v1.1, AI_LOG highlights>. Use short
headings. Do not invent numbers, features or users. Mark anything you are unsure about with [CHECK].
```
**Verify the output by:** checking every number and claim against your evidence list and deleting
anything you cannot show in the repository. If a claim has no link to a file, test or run, cut it.
Watch for over-claims ("handles millions of requests", "never fails"): replace them with what you
measured and what you designed for.

### Prompt 2: Mock system-design interview
```text
Act as a backend interviewer. Ask me 8 questions about this rate limiter, one at a time, from easy to
hard, based on this README, the threat list and the ADRs: <paste>. Include follow-ups about scale,
Redis failure, clock drift and Redis Cluster. After each answer, tell me what a strong answer would add.
Start now with question 1.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking its "strong answers" against your ADRs, the Redis documentation
(EVAL and scripting, `TIME`, Cluster key hash tags, `SCAN`), the IETF draft on RateLimit header fields and
RFC 9457. An interviewer persona can still be wrong about details.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] README case study with real evidence and links.
- [ ] `docs/retrospective.md`.
- [ ] AI usage summary (three bullets) in the README, backed by `AI_LOG.md`.
- [ ] A recorded 2-minute walkthrough (optional, but recommended).

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Which README claim is strongest?
- [ ] "Enterprise-grade, infinitely scalable rate limiting."
- [ ] "Uses Redis best practices."
- [x] "400 parallel checks over two instances against a limit of 100: exactly 100 allowed, p95 under 10 ms, proven by scripts/load-test.py and an integration test (link)."
- [ ] "Built with AI."
> **Answer:** Specific, verifiable, linked. Reviewers trust evidence, not adjectives.

### Q2. What belongs in "What I'd do next"?
- [x] Concrete, prioritised improvements with a reason (e.g. Redis Sentinel, because the game day showed Redis is the single point of failure and fail modes only soften it)
- [ ] Everything that is missing
- [ ] Apologies for unfinished work
- [ ] Nothing, it signals weakness
> **Answer:** Knowing the next steps and why shows judgement, and gives the interviewer something to discuss.

### Q3. How should you describe AI use in your portfolio?
- [ ] Hide it
- [ ] Claim the AI wrote everything
- [x] Honestly, with examples of what you verified, changed and rejected
- [ ] Only mention it if asked
> **Answer:** Responsible AI use is a skill employers look for. Your AI_LOG is the evidence.

### Q4. An interviewer asks "What happens when Redis hangs?" Which answer is best?
- [ ] "Redis is in memory, so it does not hang."
- [ ] "Requests fail until it comes back."
- [x] "After three timeouts a circuit breaker stops calling Redis for 5 s, and each tenant's failMode decides: 503, allow, or a local per-instance limit; health stays 200 DEGRADED. A game day measured v1.0 answering every check after a 1 s timeout and v1.1 answering in a few milliseconds."
- [ ] "I would use a bigger Redis."
> **Answer:** Describe the designed behaviour, how you proved it (tests + game day), and what you learned
> (correct but slow is still an incident, see the reference post-mortem).

### Q5. Which retrospective item is most useful?
- [ ] "Distributed systems are hard."
- [x] "Our failure tests used a stopped Redis; next time we also test a frozen one and assert a latency budget for the 503."
- [ ] "Everything went well."
- [ ] "The AI made mistakes."
> **Answer:** A good retrospective item names a specific cause and a concrete, testable change.

## 7. What you learned
- Turning a project into a case study backed by evidence, including correctness and security evidence.
- Running a retrospective and extracting transferable lessons.
- Communicating trade-offs and AI usage clearly and honestly.
- The full lifecycle: requirements and threats → design → implementation → tests → CI/CD → operations → reflection.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git show phase-8-end:README.md | less           # reference case study
git show phase-8-end:docs/retrospective.md
git diff phase-7-end phase-8-end --stat         # docs only
```
